Department of the Treasury

26 CFR Part 1
[TD 10059]
RIN 1545-BJ87
AGENCY:
Internal Revenue Service (IRS), Treasury.
ACTION:
Final regulations.
SUMMARY:
This document contains final regulations clarifying that, in the case of certain transfers between members of a consolidated group, a transferee's assumption of certain liabilities will not reduce the transferor's basis in the transferee's stock received in the transfer. These final regulations affect consolidated groups and their members.
DATES:
Effective date:
These final regulations are effective on October 16, 2026.
Applicability date:
For the date of applicability,
see
§ 1.1502-80(d)(4).
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
William W. Burhop at (202) 317-5363 (not a toll-free number).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority
The final regulations contained in this Treasury decision are issued under the authority of section 1502 of the Internal Revenue Code (Code), which authorizes the Secretary of the Treasury or the Secretary's delegate (Secretary) to prescribe regulations for an affiliated group of corporations that join in filing (or that are required to join in filing) a consolidated return (consolidated group) to clearly reflect, and to prevent the avoidance of, the Federal income tax liability of the consolidated group. For purposes of carrying out those objectives, section 1502 authorizes the Secretary to prescribe rules that may be different from the provisions of chapter 1 of the Code (chapter 1) that would apply if the corporations composing the consolidated group filed separate returns.
Additionally, these regulations are issued pursuant to section 7805(a) of the Code, which authorizes the Secretary to prescribe all needful rules and regulations for the enforcement of the Code, including all rules and regulations as may be necessary by reason of any alteration of law in relation to internal revenue.
Background
I. Overview
This Treasury decision contains final regulations that revise the Income Tax Regulations (
26 CFR part 1
) issued under the authority of section 1502 (consolidated return regulations) to clarify that, in the case of certain transfers between members of a consolidated group, a transferee member's assumption of liabilities to which section 357(c) of the Code applies will not reduce the transferor member's basis in the transferee member's stock received in the transfer. Terms used in the consolidated return regulations generally are defined in § 1.1502-1.
II. Section 1.1502-80
Section 1.1502-80, which was promulgated on March 18, 1992 (
see
TD 8402,
57 FR 9385
), provides rules regarding the applicability of provisions of law other than the consolidated
(
printed page 65684)
return regulations to a consolidated group. Section 1.1502-80(a)(1) generally provides that: (i) the Code, or other law, is applicable to a consolidated group to the extent the consolidated return regulations do not exclude its application; and (ii) to the extent not excluded, other rules operate in addition to, and may be modified by, the consolidated return regulations.
Section 1.1502-80(d)(1) provides that section 357(c) does not apply to any transaction to which § 1.1502-13 (or predecessor sections of the consolidated return regulations) applies, including intragroup section 351 exchanges (that is, exchanges between members of a consolidated group to which section 351 of the Code applies). Following the promulgation of § 1.1502-80(d)(1), a question arose regarding the timing of basis reductions under section 358 with respect to liabilities generally excluded from the application of section 357(c) under section 357(c)(3).
Accordingly, on November 14, 2001, the Department of the Treasury (Treasury Department) and the IRS published a notice of proposed rulemaking (REG-137519-01) in the
Federal Register
(
66 FR 57021
) that would have modified the consolidated return regulations to clarify that, in intragroup section 351 exchanges, a transferee's assumption of certain liabilities described in section 357(c)(3) would not reduce the transferor's basis in the transferee's stock received in the transfer (2001 proposed regulations).
III. 2023 Proposed Regulations and 2024 Proposed Regulations
On August 7, 2023, the Treasury Department and the IRS published a notice of proposed rulemaking (REG-134420-10) in the
Federal Register
(
88 FR 52057
) that primarily proposed to revise the consolidated return regulations to (i) eliminate obsolete or otherwise outdated provisions, (ii) modernize the language and improve the clarity of the regulations, and (iii) facilitate taxpayer compliance (2023 proposed regulations). However, the 2023 proposed regulations also withdrew the 2001 proposed regulations.
On December 30, 2024, the Treasury Department and the IRS published a notice of proposed rulemaking (REG-134420-10) in the
Federal Register
(
89 FR 106884
) that reproposed the approach under the 2001 proposed regulations to clarify the Treasury Department's and IRS's view regarding the appropriate timing for the single basis reduction for an assumed liability described in section 357(c)(3)(A) (2024 proposed regulations).
Summary of Comments and Explanation of Revisions
The Treasury Department and the IRS requested comments on the 2024 proposed regulations. No comments were received, and no public hearing was requested or held. Accordingly, the 2024 proposed regulations are adopted with non-substantive revisions to (i) clarify the applicability date, and (ii) remove an example that is no longer relevant after amendments made to section 357(c)(1)(B) by the American Jobs Creation Act of 2004,
Public Law 108-357
,  898(b), 118 Stat. 1418, 1649 (2004).
Applicability Date
Pursuant to section 1503(a) of the Code, the amendments made by this Treasury decision to the regulations issued under the authority of section 1502 apply to consolidated return years for which the due date of the return (without regard to extensions) is after October 16, 2026.
Special Analyses
I. Regulatory Planning and Review
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety effects, distributive impacts, and equity).
Executive Order 13563
emphasizes the importance of quantifying both costs and benefits, reducing costs, harmonizing rules, and promoting flexibility.
These regulations are not subject to review under section 6(b) of
Executive Order 12866
pursuant to the Memorandum of Agreement (July 4, 2025) between the Treasury Department and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) regarding review of tax regulations.
II. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
) (PRA) generally requires that a Federal agency obtain the approval of the OMB before collecting information from the public, whether that collection of information is mandatory, voluntary, or required to obtain or retain a benefit. An agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless it displays a valid control number assigned by the OMB.
These regulations amend the consolidated return regulations to clarify the timing of a single basis adjustment required by statute. Therefore, these final regulations do not impose additional reporting burden beyond what is otherwise required by existing statutes, regulations, and forms. Any general recordkeeping requirements imposed by these regulations are considered general tax records under § 1.6001-1(e). For purposes of the PRA, these general tax records already are approved under OMB control number 1545-0123.
III. Regulatory Flexibility Act
Pursuant to the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. chapter 6
), it is hereby certified that these regulations will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. This certification is based on the fact that these regulations only apply to corporations that join in filing consolidated Federal income tax returns and that such corporations tend to be larger businesses. Specifically, based on data available to the IRS, corporations that file consolidated Federal income tax returns represent only approximately two percent of all filers of Forms 1120 (
U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return
). However, these consolidated Federal income tax returns account for approximately 95 percent of the aggregate amount of receipts reported on all Forms 1120. Therefore, these final regulations would not create significant additional obligations for, or impose an economic impact on, a substantial number of small entities. Accordingly, the Secretary certifies that these regulations will not have significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
IV. Submission to the Small Business Administration
Pursuant to section 7805(f) of the Code, the notice of proposed rulemaking that preceded these final regulations was submitted to the Chief Counsel for the Office of Advocacy of the Small Business Administration for comment on its impact on small business. No comments were received from the Chief Counsel for the Office of Advocacy of the Small Business Administration.
V. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits and take certain other actions before issuing a final rule that includes any Federal mandate that may result in expenditures in any one year by a State, local, or Tribal government, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated
(
printed page 65685)
annually for inflation. These regulations do not include any Federal mandate that may result in expenditures by State, local, or Tribal governments, or by the private sector, in excess of that threshold.
VI.
Executive Order 13132
: Federalism
Executive Order 13132
(Federalism) prohibits an agency from publishing any rule that has federalism implications if the rule either imposes substantial, direct compliance costs on State and local governments, and is not required by statute, or preempts State law, unless the agency meets the consultation and funding requirements of section 6 of the Executive order. These regulations do not have federalism implications, do not impose substantial direct compliance costs on State and local governments, and do not preempt State law within the meaning of the Executive order.
VII. Congressional Review Act
Pursuant to the Congressional Review Act (
5 U.S.C. 801
et seq.
), the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs designated this rule as not a major rule, as defined by
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
.
Drafting Information
The principal author of these regulations is William W. Burhop of the Office of Associate Chief Counsel (Corporate). However, other personnel from the Treasury Department and the IRS participated in their development.

Par. 2.
Section 1.1502-80 is amended by:
1.

The revisions and additions read as follows:
§ 1.1502-80
Applicability of other provisions of law.
*
*
*
*
*
(d) * * *
(1)
In general
—(i)
General rule.
Section 357(c) does not apply to any transaction to which § 1.1502-13 applies. Notwithstanding the foregoing, for purposes of determining the transferor's basis in property under section 358(a) received in a transfer described in section 351, section 358(d)(2) operates to exclude liabilities described in section 357(c)(3)(A), other than those also described in section 357(c)(3)(B), from the computation of the amount of liabilities assumed that is treated as money received under section 358(d)(1).
(ii)
Application.
This paragraph (d) does not apply to a transaction if the transferor or transferee becomes a nonmember as part of the same plan or arrangement. The transferor (or transferee) is treated as becoming a nonmember once it is no longer a member of a consolidated group that includes the transferee (or transferor). For purposes of this paragraph (d), any reference to a transferor or transferee includes, as the context may require, a reference to a successor or predecessor.
(2)
Tax years beginning before January 1, 1995.
* * *
(3)
Example
—(i)
Facts.
P owns all the stock of S1. S1 has assets with a total fair market value equal to $100 and an aggregate basis of $30. S1 has $40 of liabilities, $5 of which are described in section 357(c)(3)(A) but not section 357(c)(3)(B), and $35 of which are not described in section 357(c)(3)(A). S1 transfers its assets to a newly formed subsidiary, S2, in exchange for stock of S2 and S2's assumption of the $40 of liabilities in a transaction to which section 351 applies. P, S1, and S2 are members of a consolidated group.
(ii)
Analysis.
Section 357(c) does not apply to cause S1 to recognize gain in connection with the transfer. For purposes of determining S1's basis in the S2 stock it received in the exchange, section 358(d)(2) operates to exclude $5 of the liabilities from the computation of the amount of liabilities assumed that are treated as money received under section 358(d)(1). S1's basis in the S2 stock received in the exchange is a $5 excess loss account (reflecting its $30 basis in the assets transferred reduced by $35, the amount of liabilities assumed that are not described in section 357(c)(3)(A)).
(4)
Applicability dates.
Paragraphs (d)(1) and (3) of this section apply to transactions occurring in consolidated return years for which the due date of the return (without regard to extensions) is after October 16, 2026. For rules that apply to transactions occurring in earlier taxable years,
see
§ 1.1502-80(d) as contained in
26 CFR part 1
, revised April 1, 2026.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is proposing to establish a temporary safety zone for navigable waters on the Cumberland River from mile marker 221.7 to 222. The safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with an overwater fireworks display. This proposed rulemaking would prohibit persons and vessels from being in the safety zone unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Ohio Valley, or their designated representative.
DATES:
Comments and related material must be received by the Coast Guard on or before October 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
To submit comments and view available documents, go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and search for USCG-2026-1075.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have questions about this proposed rule, contact MST2 Jason Brincefield, MSD Nashville Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone (206) 815-7006, or email
MSDNashville@uscg.mil
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations
CFR Code of Federal Regulations
COTP Captain of the Port
DHS Department of Homeland Security
FR Federal Register
NPRM Notice of proposed rulemaking
§ Section
U.S.C. United States Code
II. Background and Authority
On July 17, 2026, an organization notified the Coast Guard that they will be sponsoring an event where fireworks will be launched from a barge on the Cumberland River Mile Marker 221.7-222 near Sanders Ferry Park. The event will begin with a morning fireworks display on October 29, 2026, from approximately 7:30 a.m. to 8 a.m., and will conclude with a second fireworks display on October 31, 2026, from approximately 5 p.m. through 5:15 p.m. The safety zone will be enforced for a period of time before and after the fireworks displays to ensure safety during staging and at the end of the fireworks. The safety zone will be enforced from 6 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. on October 29, 2026, and from 4 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. on October 30, 2026. This event and associated fireworks displays are expected to draw a large number of spectator craft.
The Captain of the Port, Ohio Valley (COTP) is issuing safety zone under the authority in
46 U.S.C. 70034
. The COTP has determined that potential hazards with the fireworks displays include the launch of explosive projectiles, falling debris, and potential for vessel collisions. The purpose of this rulemaking is to protect event spectators and transiting vessels before, during, and after the scheduled fireworks displays.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This proposed rule would establish a safety zone from 6:30 a.m. on October 29, 2026, until 6:30 p.m. on October 31, 2026. The safety zone would only be enforced from 6:30 a.m. to 9 a.m. on October 29, 2026, and from 4 p.m. until 6:30 p.m. on October 31, 2026. The safety zone would cover all navigable waters on the Cumberland River from mile marker 221.7 to 222. No vessel or person would be permitted to enter the safety zone without obtaining permission from the COTP or their designated representative. The regulatory text we are proposing appears at the end of this document.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this proposed rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analyses based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980,
5 U.S.C. 601-612
, as amended, requires Federal agencies to consider the potential impact of regulations on small entities during rulemaking. The term “small entities” comprises small businesses, not-for-profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000. The Coast Guard certifies under
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
that this proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities for the following reasons.
Although vessel traffic would not be able to transit around this regulated area, the regulation would only impact a small area for approximately 2.5 hours each day. The Coast Guard would issue a Broadcast Notice to Marines via VHF FM marine channel 16, which would allow small entities to adjust their transit plans, and the rule allows vessels to request permission to enter the regulated area from the COTP.
If you think that your business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction qualifies as a small entity and that this proposed rule would have a significant economic impact on it, please submit a comment (see
ADDRESSES
) explaining why you think it qualifies and how and to what degree this proposed rule would economically affect it.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (
Pub. L. 104-121
), if this proposed rule would affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions, contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section. Small businesses may send comments to the Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and the Regional Small Business Regulatory Fairness Boards by calling 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247).
B. Collection of Information
This proposed rule would not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this proposed rule under
Executive Order 13132
, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.
Also, this proposed rule does not have tribal implications under
Executive Order 13175
, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because it does not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship
(
printed page 65699)
between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
As required by The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
), the Coast Guard certifies that this proposed rule would not result in an annual expenditure of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted for inflation) by a State, local, or tribal government, in the aggregate, or by the private sector.
E. Environment
We have analyzed this proposed rule under Department of Homeland Security Directive 023-01, Rev. 1, associated implementing instructions, and Environmental Planning COMDTINST 5090.1 (series), which guide the Coast Guard in complying with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
), and have determined that this action is one of a category of actions that do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment. This proposed rule is a safety zone. It is categorically excluded from further review under paragraph L60(a).
V. Public Participation and Request for Comments
We view public participation as essential to effective rulemaking and will consider all comments and material received during the comment period. Your comment can help shape the outcome of this rulemaking. If you submit a comment, please include the docket number for this rulemaking, indicate the specific section of this document to which each comment applies, and provide a reason for each suggestion or recommendation.

§ 165.T899-1075
Safety Zone; Cumberland River, Hendersonville, TN
(a)
Location.
This safety zone applies to the following regulated area: all waters of the Cumberland River from mile marker 221.7 to 222.
(b)
Definitions.
As used in this section, designated representative means a Coast Guard Patrol Commander, including a Coast Guard coxswain, petty officer, or other officer operating a Coast Guard vessel and a Federal, State, and local officer designated by or assisting the COTP, Ohio Valley in the enforcement of the regulated area.

(d)
Enforcement period.
This section will be enforced on October 29, 2026, from 6:30 a.m. to 9 a.m., and October 31, 2026, from 4 p.m. to 6:30 p.m.

SUMMARY:
NMFS is reallocating the projected unused amount of the 2026 Atka mackerel incidental catch allowance (ICA) for the Bering Sea subarea and Eastern Aleutian district (BS/EAI) to the Amendment 80 cooperative allocation for the BS/EAI in the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands management area (BSAI). This action is necessary to allow the 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of Atka mackerel in the BS/EAI to be fully harvested.
DATES:
Effective October 16, 2026 through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Steve Whitney, 907-586-7228.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the
(
printed page 65695)
BSAI according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands Management Area (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of
50 CFR part 600
and
50 CFR part 679
.
The 2026 Atka mackerel ICA for the BSAI trawl limited access sector and the non-trawl gear sector for the BS/EAI is 800 metric tons (mt) and the 2026 Atka mackerel TAC allocated to the Amendment 80 sector for the BS/EAI is 32,819 mt as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the BSAI (
91 FR 11750
, March 10, 2026). For 2026, all Amendment 80 vessels are part of the sole Amendment 80 cooperative, so the TAC allocated to the Amendment 80 sector is allocated entirely to the sole Amendment 80 cooperative and no TAC is assigned to the Amendment 80 limited access fishery.
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS has determined that 700 mt of the Atka mackerel ICA for the BS/EAI will not be harvested. Therefore, in accordance with § 679.91(f), NMFS reallocates 700 mt of Atka mackerel from the BS/EAI ICA to the BS/EAI Amendment 80 cooperative allocation in the BS/EAI. In accordance with § 679.91(f), NMFS will reissue the cooperative quota permit for the reallocated Atka mackerel following the procedures set forth in § 679.91(f)(3).

AGENCY:
Office of Administration, Executive Office of the President.
ACTION:
Notice of availability; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
Consistent with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) and Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966, as amended (NHPA), this Notice announces the availability and opportunity for public review and comment of a draft Environmental Assessment (EA), which examines the potential impacts of a proposal by the Office of Administration (OA), Executive Office of the President (EOP), to improve the granite façade of the Dwight D. Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB). Pursuant to this notice, OA is also seeking public comment on the potential of the proposed improvements to cause adverse effects on historic properties. Finally, this notice provides information on how individuals and organizations may request to become consulting parties.
DATES:
This notice initiates a public comment period for the Draft EA. OA requests that the public submit comments concerning the scope of the analysis, potential alternatives, and identification of relevant information and studies by November 16, 2026. To afford OA the opportunity to consider comments, please ensure any comments are received prior to the close of the 30-day comment period.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments, identified by docket number OA-2026-0001, by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov/​docket/​OA-2026-0001
.
Email:
FedRegComments@oa.eop.gov
. Include docket number OA-2026-0001 in the subject line of the message.
Instructions:
All submissions received outside of
Regulations.gov
must include the name “Office of Administration” and the docket number for this notice of availability. OA makes all comments, including the names, addresses, and other personally identifiable information included in the comment, available for public review online. Individuals can request that OA withhold their names, addresses, or other personally identifiable information included in their comment from the public record; however, OA cannot guarantee that it will be able to do so.
All submissions from organizations or businesses and from individuals identifying themselves as representatives or officials of organizations or businesses will be made available for public inspection in their entirety.
Supporting documents and any comments we receive on this docket may be viewed at
https://www.regulations.gov/​docket/​OA-2026-0001
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Office of Administration, Heather Martin, Deputy Director and Chief Financial Officer, (202) 456-4646,
FedRegNotices@oa.eop.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Introduction
The Draft EA evaluates the potential environmental impacts of a proposal by OA to make improvements to the granite façade of the EEOB and bring it into visual alignment with the neighboring White House. Section 590 of Public Law 100-461 authorizes the OA Director to accept gifts, property, and voluntary services to support renovation and rehabilitation of the EEOB, and establishes a United States Treasury Fund for those purposes. OA is not a Federal agency and is therefore is not required to comply with either NEPA or the NHPA. Moreover, given the EEOB's location on White House grounds, it is exempt from the requirements of the NHPA under Section 107. Nonetheless, OA is voluntarily following the NEPA and NHPA procedures for this Project because those procedures provide a generally well-understood framework for considering potential effects and receiving input from agencies, the public, and interested parties.
Purpose of and Need for the Proposed Action
The subject of the Project, the EEOB, is located to the west of the White House at 17th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue NW. The Project is proposed to rehabilitate and improve the granite façade of the EEOB to restore and beautify its physical appearance, consistent with
Executive Order 14344
, Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again. At present, several areas of the EEOB's façade are deteriorating, including through granular disintegration, delamination, incipient spalling, cracking, and chipping, as well as gypsum salt accumulation, efflorescence, stains from exposure to contaminants, and biological growth. This deterioration has worsened over time and diminished the EEOB's appearance and stature. Further, the gray façade of the EEOB, combined with its size and massing, conveys a dark, drab, and uninspiring presence that detracts from the aesthetic presentation of the much smaller White House directly adjacent to it. In carrying out proposed exterior improvements, OA proposes to address existing areas of degradation, engage in various masonry preservation measures, and coat the façade with white, mineral silicate paint. The proposed action would not only address areas of disrepair on the EEOB's façade, but would also visually align the EEOB with the White House, of which it is a functional extension.
Alternatives Under Consideration
The EA will consider three Action Alternatives (
i.e.,
the Exterior Painting Alternative, the Partial Painting Alternative, and the Cleaning and Lighting Alternative) and the No Action Alternative. Under the Exterior Painting Alternative (the “Preferred Alternative”), the EEOB's whole granite façade (excluding interior courtyards) would be painted with a white, mineral silicate paint. Prior to painting, the granite facade would be prepared for
(
printed page 65715)
painting, which would include a conservation-based cleaning regimen and stone repair and preservation measures implemented in accordance with the Secretary of Interior's Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties. Façade lighting also would be installed. The Partial Painting Alternative involves painting only the exterior granite walls of the upper floors of all four elevations, leaving the raised foundation (currently a different type, texture, and shade of granite) unpainted. As with the Preferred Alternative, the paint would be a shade of white, mineral silicate paint, the courtyard elevations would remain unpainted, the exterior walls would undergo cleaning and stone repair prior to painting, and façade lighting would be installed. The Cleaning and Lighting Alternative involves only cleaning the exterior granite using a gentle, conservation-based cleaning method to remove dirt and soiling on all four exterior elevations, to remove unattractive stains, and to improve the overall appearance of the exterior facade. Under the No Action Alternative, cleaning and painting of the EEOB façade would not occur. Weathering and deterioration of the building façade would continue, and the aesthetics of the building would remain unaligned with that of the White House.
OA welcomes comments on all four alternatives, as well as suggestions for additional alternatives.
Public Input and Consultation
This notice of availability provides a period for the public to identify issues and potential alternatives for consideration. Federal agencies; state, tribal, and local governments; and the general public will have the opportunity to assist OA in identifying the following for analysis: historic properties that could be affected by the Project, potential adverse effects, reasonable alternatives, and potential mitigation measures to be analyzed.
OA will use the NEPA coordination process provided for in the NHPA regulations (
36 CFR 800.8
). OA will consider all written requests from individuals or organizations to participate as consulting parties under NHPA and, as discussed below, will determine who among those parties will be a consulting party in accordance with NHPA regulations.
NHPA Consulting Parties:
Certain individuals and organizations with a demonstrated interest in the Project can request to participate as NHPA consulting parties under
36 CFR 800.2(c)(5)
, due to the nature of their legal or economic relation to the undertaking or affected properties, or their concern with the undertaking's effects on historic properties.
Interested individuals or organizations can request to be consulting parties by emailing:
ConsultingParties@oa.eop.gov
.
Parties requesting consulting status should provide all information that would allow OA to fully evaluate the request. OA will determine which interested parties should be consulting parties.
Comments:
Federal agencies; tribal, state, and local governments; and other interested parties are requested to comment on the scope of this EA, significant issues that should be addressed, and alternatives that should be considered. For information on how to submit comments, see the
ADDRESSES
section above.

42 U.S.C. 4321-4347

Deputy Director and Chief Financial Officer.

AGENCY:
Office of Adjudication, Recruitment, and Management, Justice Management Division, Department of Justice.
ACTION:
60-Day notice.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Attorney Recruitment and Management (OARM), Justice Management Division (JMD), Department of Justice (DOJ), will be submitting the following information collection request to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995.
DATES:
Comments are encouraged and will be accepted for 60 days until December 15, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have additional comments especially on the estimated public burden or associated response time, suggestions, or need a copy of the proposed information collection instrument with instructions or additional information, please contact Michael E. Stamp, Office of Adjudication, Recruitment, and Management, 450 5th St. NW, Suite 10200, (202) 514-3905.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Written comments and suggestions from the public and affected agencies concerning the proposed collection of information are encouraged. Your comments should address one or more of the following four points:
—Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the (component), including whether the information will have practical utility;

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
We published a
Federal Register
Notice with a 60-day public comment period on this information collection on August 12, 2026, at [
91 FR 52108
]. The notice received two comments. The comments and FHWA's responses are below:
The comments received by the recipient include (1) Is the collection necessary?; (2) Is the burden estimate accurate?; (3) Ways to enhance the quality and clarity of the collected information; and (4) Ways to limit burden without reducing the quality of the collected information.
FHWA appreciates the feedback and understands that this could require extra work from the States. Unfortunately, because of the complexity of our programs, we rely heavily on the States to provide the requested information. Since each State operates differently, the grant accrual calculation and process consolidate all State responses and FHWA uses a standardized process to calculate the quarterly grant accrual to compensate for the differences.
The burden is our best guess at how much time it takes a State to complete the annual survey. However, burden on the States depends on several factors. Several factor examples include State personnel (new vs seasoned employee), familiarity with completing the annual survey (1st time versus 7th time), and knowledge of the Federal grants management process and procedures. However, we have taken steps to reduce the burden by States to research variances. The steps taken by FHWA include providing the States with the program and projects that make up the variance.
We are continuously enhancing our grants process so that the estimate on our financial statements is conservative, yet appropriate for the fiscal year end reporting to meet the Departmental, financial statement auditors, and Federal government-wide expectations. This estimate is required per the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles as well as other accounting authoritative sources.
We do welcome and value your feedback. We will keep your comments in mind when we further enhance our quarterly grant accrual process.
Title:
Annual Grants State Survey & Quarterly Lookback Analysis.
Background:
Respondents are required to answer 29 questions regarding Federal-aid grant payments and billing cycles. FHWA reviews the prior fiscal year (FY) survey questions to determine if updates are required based on the Departmental OIG external financial statement audit and/or process changes and improvements. The survey is sent out annually to the division offices/States in the May/June timeframe. The survey responses are due from the division offices/States to FHWA in the July/August timeframe.
The responses from the annual survey are key inputs to calculating the quarterly grant accrual for the Federal-aid program by States. The responses are updated in the grant accrual data analytics Excel workbook file by State, program, project, and other data attributes. The estimated quarterly grant accrual is compared to the subsequent quarter's disbursements to validate the effectiveness of the quarterly grant accrual calculation referred to as the lookback analysis. States with a $50 million dollar variance and at least +/− 20% variance or more are required to provide FHWA with an explanation. FHWA reviews the responses from the division offices/States for adequacy, and if required, and sends a follow-up email to the division offices/States to provide additional information. Approximately seven States are required to provide a variance explanation. FHWA identifies the programs and projects that make up the variance. States are only required to provide explanations for the programs and projects that make up the variance. The number of required explanations is approximately ten per quarter per State. In total, FHWA reviews approximately 70 variance explanations per quarter.
The quarterly lookback analysis and the data analytics are used to analyze payment trends, make enhancements to the grant accrual process, provide reasonable estimates for the grant liabilities and expenses, satisfy accounting principles and guidance requirements, and provide support for internal and external audits. The quarterly grant accrual calculations and the lookback analyses are performed for quarters 1-4.
Respondents:
50 State DOTs and District of Columbia.
Frequency:
Annually for the Grants State Survey and Quarterly for the Lookback Analysis.
Estimated Average Burden per Response:
5.32 hours per respondent per application per form.
Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours:
The total burden hours for States are 1,951.15 hours (271.15 hours for annual grants State survey and 1,680 hours for four lookback analysis quarters).
Public Comments Invited:
You are asked to comment on any aspect of this information collection, including: (1) Whether the proposed collection is necessary for the FHWA's performance; (2) the accuracy of the estimated burdens; (3) ways for the FHWA to enhance the quality, usefulness, and clarity of the collected information; and (4) ways that the burden could be minimized, including the use of electronic technology, without reducing the quality of the collected information. The agency will summarize and/or include your comments in the request for OMB's clearance of this information collection.

title: Notice of Availability of a Pest Risk Analysis for the Interstate Movement of Fresh Leaves and Rhizomes of Wasabi From Hawaii Into the Continental United States
abstract: We are advising the public that we have prepared a pest risk analysis that evaluates the risks associated with the interstate movement of fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi (Eutrema japonicum) for consumption from Hawaii into the continental United States. The interstate movement of fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi from Hawaii into the continental United States is not currently authorized. Based on the findings of the pest risk analysis, we have determined that the application of one or more designated phytosanitary measures will be sufficient to mitigate the risks of introducing or disseminating plant pests or noxious weeds via the interstate movement of fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi from Hawaii. We are making the pest risk analysis available to the public for review and comment.
dates: We will consider all comments that we receive on or before December 15, 2026.

, referred to below as the regulations), the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) prohibits or restricts the movement in interstate commerce of any plant or plant product from Hawaii and the Territories to prevent plant pests or noxious weeds from being introduced into or disseminated within the United States.
Section 318.13-4 contains a performance-based process for authorizing the interstate movement of certain fruits and vegetables from Hawaii and the Territories that, based on the findings of a pest risk analysis, can be safely moved interstate subject to one or more of the five designated phytosanitary measures listed in paragraph (b) of that section.
APHIS received a request from the State of Hawaii to allow the interstate movement of fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi (
Eutrema japonicum
) from Hawaii into the continental United States. As part of our evaluation of Hawaii's request, we have prepared a pest risk assessment to identify the pests of quarantine significance that could follow the pathway of the interstate movement of fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi into the continental United States from Hawaii. Based on the pest risk assessment, a risk management document (RMD) was prepared to identify phytosanitary measures that could be applied to the fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi to mitigate the pest risk.
Therefore, in accordance with § 318.13-4(c), we are announcing the availability of our pest risk assessment and RMD for public review and comment. Those documents, as well as a description of the economic considerations associated with the interstate movement of fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi from Hawaii, may be viewed on the
Regulations.gov
website or in our reading room (see
ADDRESSES
above for a link to
Regulations.gov
and information on the location and hours of the reading room). You may request paper copies of the pest risk assessment and RMD by calling or writing to the person listed under
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
. Please refer to the subject of the analysis you wish to review when requesting copies.
After reviewing any comments we receive, we will announce our decision regarding the interstate movement status of fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi from Hawaii in a subsequent notice. If the overall conclusions of our analysis and the Administrator's determination of risk remain unchanged following our consideration of the comments, then we will authorize the interstate movement of fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi from Hawaii into the continental United States subject to the requirements specified in the RMD.

AGENCY:
National Park Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The National Park Service (NPS) amends special regulations for Denali National Park and Preserve to conform the regulations regarding the number of vehicles that can travel on the restricted section of the Denali Park Road (miles 15-90) to a Vehicle Management Plan that the NPS has been implementing since 2012. This rule implements the plan's limit that no more than 160 vehicles may travel on the restricted section of the road per 24-hour period during the visitor season (also referred to as the “allocation season”), defined in the park's General Management Plan as beginning on the Saturday before Memorial Day and ending on the second Thursday after Labor Day. This limit allows the NPS to meet growing visitor demand while maintaining a high-quality experience for visitors.
DATES:
This rule is effective November 16, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Comments received on the proposed rule are available on
https://www.regulations.gov
in Docket No. NPS-2026-0067. A copy of the Denali Park Road Vehicle Management Plan and Environmental Impact Statement and related Record of Decision provide information and context for this rule and are available online at
https://parkplanning.nps.gov/​dena
by clicking the link titled “Denali Park Road Vehicle Management Plan” and then the link titled “Document List.”
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Brooke Merrell, Superintendent, Denali National Park and Preserve; (907) 683-9581;
brooke_merrell@nps.gov
.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Denali Park Road and Vehicle Management Plan
In 1917, Congress established Mount McKinley National Park as a “game refuge” with the intent that it be “set apart as a public park for the benefit and enjoyment of the people” (39 Stat. 938). In 1980, Congress passed the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA, Pub. L. 96-487), which enlarged and renamed the park Denali National Park and Preserve. A general purpose of all ANILCA lands is to preserve them for the benefit, use, education and inspiration of present and future generations.
16 U.S.C. 3101(a)
. The Denali Park Road (“park road”) serves both of these purposes. Built over 16 years (1922-1938), the historic 92-mile park road is an important means of access to the park and is one of the best places in the world for the public to observe large northern mammals in their natural habitat. Visitors traveling the park road often observe Dall sheep, caribou, wolves, grizzly bears, moose, and foxes. Nowhere else in America can visitors observe such concentrations of these large species of wildlife in such an accessible natural setting. Visitors traveling the road also have many opportunities to observe smaller mammals and birds, some of which are rarely seen elsewhere in North America. Alaska Range features, such as glacially carved mountains, Mount McKinley, and the open views of dynamic alpine landscapes, also are a source of visitor enjoyment and inspiration. The park road facilitates wilderness recreational opportunities and supports freedom of discovery, a sense of adventure, and a connection to nature.
The NPS's ability to balance the protection of park resources while offering quality visitor experiences is exemplified in the management of the park road. Road crews use graders and haul gravel to maintain it, rangers patrol it, and commercial services staff manage the transportation concession contract for it, so visitors can ride buses to view wildlife and access the park's wilderness. In 2012, planning staff, with
(
printed page 65691)
public input, worked to create the Denali Park Road Vehicle Management Plan and Environmental Impact Statement (VMP), which adopted an adaptive management strategy that includes measurable indicators and standards for visitor experience and resource protection.
[
1
]
These include crowding standards for the number of vehicles at wildlife stops, in a viewscape, and at a rest area; the spacing of vehicles to ensure time for sheep crossings; restrictions to night-time traffic volumes; and restrictions to large (construction-related) vehicle traffic. On September 27, 2012, the Regional Director, Alaska signed a Record of Decision (ROD) selecting the preferred alternative in the VMP for implementation. One standard in the selected alternative limits the maximum level of vehicle use on the restricted section of the park road (miles 15-90) to 160 vehicles per 24-hour period in the visitor season, defined in the park's General Management Plan (GMP) as the season beginning on the Saturday before Memorial Day and ending on the second Thursday after Labor Day. This standard allows the NPS to meet growing visitor demand while maintaining a high-quality experience. The NPS has been managing vehicle use on the park road consistent with the VMP since 2012. Resources staff monitor this and other indicators in the VMP to ensure the road is managed according to the plan.
Final Rule
This rule conforms the park's special regulations to reflect how the NPS has managed the park road since adoption of the VMP in 2012. The current version of the special regulations authorizes the NPS to issue no more than 10,512 motor vehicle permits for travel on the restricted section of the park road during the visitor season. This regulatory text will be revised to provide that no more than 160 vehicles may travel on the restricted section of the road per 24-hour period during the visitor season. The rule also makes a minor change to the regulatory text by deleting text that departs from the visitor season, as it is defined in the GMP, by ending the season on September 15 if that comes before the second Thursday after Labor Day. The rule provides that the season always ends on the second Thursday after Labor Day, providing additional opportunities for recreation and access by lengthening the season in some years. By stating the cap in terms of the number of vehicles, rather than the number of permits, the rule also clarifies that any vehicle traveling on the park road counts toward the vehicle limit, not just vehicles operating under a permit. The VMP evaluated impacts from all motor vehicle use on the road, permitted or not, and the NPS has been managing vehicle use on the park road in this way since 2012. Some vehicles that use the road do not have a permit, such as tour buses that operate under concession contracts and vehicles used by the NPS for administrative purposes.
Summary of Public Comments
The NPS published a proposed rule in the
Federal Register
on May 18, 2026 (
91 FR 28461
). The NPS accepted public comments for 60 days via the mail, hand delivery, and the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Comments were accepted through July 17, 2026. The NPS received 161 comments on the proposed rule. Overall, commenters broadly supported adaptive management as a tool for managing vehicle use on the park road. Commenters supported adaptive management as a means of ensuring protection of park resources and values in accordance with desired conditions while providing flexibility for managers to adjust operations based on science-driven modeling, monitoring, and observed resource or visitor-use issues. Commenters supported regulatory flexibility that allows the NPS to respond to changing conditions, monitoring results, and evolving resource needs.
After considering public comments and additional review of the proposed rule, the NPS is making several minor changes in the final rule. Two changes better reflect how the NPS has managed vehicle access on the park road under the VMP since 2012. The first change removes language held over from the existing regulations that each permit allows one vehicle one entry onto the restricted portion of the park road. The NPS issues some permits, such as construction permits, that allow for more than one entry as needed for the authorized use. The sentence in the proposed rule that followed, which stated that other forms of written authorization may have different terms and conditions, was in reference to the sentence before and therefore also has been removed. The second change reflects that vehicle counts are made when a vehicle passes westward through the gate into the restricted section of the park road. The statement in the proposed rule that no more than 160 vehicles may travel on the restricted section was imprecise and has been replaced with a statement that no more than 160 vehicles may enter the restricted section of the park road. A similar change has been made to the title of § 13.932. If the same vehicle passes through the gate more than once per day, each passage through the gate counts toward the 160 vehicle per day limit. Finally, the titles of § 13.930 and § 13.932 and the definition of the restricted section § 13.930 have been revised to clarify that the regulations in those sections only apply to vehicle use on the restricted section of the park road during the visitor season. The restricted section of the park road outside of the visitor season is determined by the NPS. As stated in § 13.936 of the existing regulations, travel on the restricted section of the park road at any time requires a permit.
A summary of the pertinent issues raised by commenters is provided below.
1. Comment:
Many commenters asked the NPS to publish vehicle management and monitoring data that can be measured against the indicators and standards in the VMP before finalizing the rule. Commenters requested information about wildlife movement and viewing, road capacity analysis and modeling, completion of a Before-After-Control-Impact (BACI) study, release of long-term monitoring datasets, impacts to wilderness character, and detailed traffic analyses (
e.g.,
daily counts, GPS vehicle tracking data, peak hour patterns, road corridor crowding, vehicle type allocation). Commenters stated that changed visitor use patterns and resource conditions since 2012, including changes caused by the closure and reopening of a large section of the park road, warrant additional review that allows the NPS to collect and analyze updated monitoring data to determine appropriate levels of vehicle use, such as through the preparation of a supplemental environmental impact statement. One commenter encouraged the NPS to regularly reassess its vehicle management framework to ensure that it uses empirical evidence to inform management decisions for more or less access.
NPS Response:
The NPS expects the visitor conditions that will exist when the park road is fully accessible to vehicle traffic in 2027 will be substantially similar to visitor conditions that existed when the scientific studies that led to the VMP were completed. Monitoring data are
(
printed page 65692)
published for 2013-2019,
[
2
]
which can be measured against the indicators and standards in the VMP. Monitoring data for 2020-2022 also are published but are not suitable for comparison to the conditions studied and tested for the VMP due to changes to visitor use patterns caused by the global pandemic and the Pretty Rocks landslide that closed the road to all vehicle traffic at mile 43 in August of 2021. The NPS is working to publish monitoring data for 2023-2025, however these data are not comparable to pre-pandemic data due to the landslide closure. The Pretty Rocks Bridge was completed in August 2026. Upon completion of the Eielson Visitor Center, the NPS monitors the indicators under “normal” traffic conditions. As resources allow, and if appropriate, the NPS may complete a BACI to affirm the selection of key indicators and to distinguish impacts due to changes in current traffic patterns and traffic levels. To the extent that future monitoring data suggest the NPS should reconsider any aspect of the adaptive management framework in the VMP, or the 160 vehicles per day cap, it will undertake all compliance and planning actions necessary to do so.
2. Comment:
Several commenters asked how the rule would affect access to private property within the park. Specifically, commenters requested that access to private property under ANILCA Sections 1110(a) and 1110(b) be exempt from vehicle caps. They also asked the NPS to clarify it cannot restrict or supersede statutory access by giving other users a transit priority, and to ensure the adaptive management framework allows for increased inholder access in response to demonstrated needs and changing conditions.
NPS Response:
The NPS will not take any action in conflict with statutory rights of access provided under Section 1110 of ANILCA.
16 U.S.C. 3170
. The NPS will ensure that its management of vehicle use on the park road, including through permit requirements or vehicle limits, will not go beyond reasonable regulation of those rights of access in accordance with Sections 1110(a) and (b).
3. Comment:
Several commenters requested that the NPS revise the rule by replacing the 160-day cap with a statement that the NPS will adaptively manage vehicle use on the park road, adjusting vehicle numbers up or down based upon monitoring data. Commenters opposed a fixed cap as unable to accommodate long-term resource conditions or evolving access needs. One commenter suggested the rule indicate that daily vehicle use is governed by the indicators and standards in the VMP and that 160 vehicles should not be a management target or baseline for use. One commenter asked the NPS to codify specific aspects of adaptive management, including requirements to publish daily vehicle counts and VMP indicator results, and to automatically reduce vehicle allocations if wildlife-stop, sheep-gap, nighttime traffic, viewscape, rest-stop, hiker-wait, or large-vehicle standards are not met.
NPS Response:
The daily vehicle cap in the rule is consistent with the VMP and will not interfere with the NPS's use of adaptive management to respond to monitoring data that indicates desired conditions are not being met. Adaptive management consistent with the VMP does not set the cap as a management goal or a desired outcome; it represents the upper bound of traffic that is allowable under the selected alternative. The NPS's experience with implementing adaptive management since adoption of the VMP in 2012 has led it to conclude that, at least as of now, it is unnecessary to codify adaptive management concepts in NPS regulations.
4. Comment:
Commenters proposed various changes to the vehicle cap in the rule, including changes that would set a seasonal rather than a daily maximum, differentiate between daytime and nighttime use, limit use to one entry and one exit on the restricted portion of the road per 24-hour period, reserve specific access opportunities for Alaska residents, and limit use to commercial tour buses. Commenters suggested changes to the number of vehicles that could travel on the park road per day, ranging from a complete prohibition on vehicle use to increasing the cap as high as 240 vehicles per day.
NPS Response:
The 160-vehicle cap is a specific standard that was selected for implementation in the ROD. The VMP includes desired conditions for daytime and nighttime use. Seasonal considerations were not a part of the scientific study leading to the VMP. However, historically and currently, there the concessionaire bus schedule is based on demand pattern which naturally creates a seasonality for the largest road user group. The bus schedule peaks in July and August. Some road permits, such as Teklanika Campground buses and concessionaire buses, are for one entry and one exit trips. Other permits, such as for construction or research projects, allow for travel back and forth along the road. Recognizing the special access provisions already provided for in ANILCA, the NPS declines to reserve additional specific access opportunities for Alaska residents in this rule.
5. Comment:
One commenter asked the NPS to consider providing additional access outside of the defined visitor season when conditions permit.
NPS Response:
The NPS already allows additional access outside the defined visitor season as conditions allow. Personal vehicles can travel on maintained portions of the park road outside of the defined visitor season between February 15 and October 15.
6. Comment:
Commenters raised concerns about potential impacts to park resources and visitors from increasing vehicle use on the park road, expressing concern that additional traffic could diminish bicycling opportunities, affect wildlife and wildlife viewing opportunities, increase pollution, degrade wilderness character, and increase the risk of accidents. One commenter stated that increased traffic would require additional road maintenance and cited studies demonstrating that heavy equipment, such as gravel-hauling trucks, can disturb wildlife and significantly reduce wildlife-viewing opportunities compared to regular vehicular traffic.
NPS Response:
The NPS will continue to monitor impacts to resources and visitor experience from vehicle use as required by the VMP. The adaptive management framework in the VMP accounts for potential impacts to a broad range of park resources and visitor experiences, including the topics raised by the commenters. The flexibility provided by adaptive management allows the NPS to adjust management actions to protect resources and visitors based upon indicators and desired conditions.
7. Comment:
Commenters raised concerns about potential impacts to NPS infrastructure and operations from increasing vehicle use on the park road, expressing concern that additional traffic would increase maintenance needs by accelerating wear on the park road, strain waste management systems, particularly the park's sewage lagoon, and require the NPS to hire or reallocate staff to support increased visitation, which would weaken the NPS's ability to ensure visitor safety, provide education, and conduct essential monitoring.
NPS Response:
There will not be impacts to the condition of the park road and infrastructure resulting from this rule such that it would require additional maintenance needs. The NPS expects that existing resources for road maintenance and wastewater will be
(
printed page 65693)
sufficient to accommodate increased visitor use given visitation trends in the park.
Compliance With Other Laws, Executive Orders, and Department Policy
Regulatory Planning and Review (Executive Orders 12866 and 14192)
This rule has been determined to be significant for purposes of
Executive Order 12866
. This rule will generate benefits for the public by providing greater clarity and transparency about the NPS's management of the park road, and by providing additional opportunities for recreation and access by lengthening the visitor season by several days in certain years. Because this rule expands recreational consumption opportunities, it is considered an “enabling regulatory action.” As a result, it is an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action. Compared to baseline conditions, this rule does not involve any fees or other measures that would increase costs to visitors, businesses, communities, or the broader public.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
This rule will not have a significant economic effect on a substantial number of small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
). This certification is based on information contained in the economic analyses found in the report entitled “[INSERT].” The report may be viewed on
https://www.regulations.gov
in Docket No. NPS-2026-0067.
Congressional Review Act
This rule is not a major rule under
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
. This rule:
(a) Will not have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more.
(b) Will not cause a major increase in costs or prices for consumers, individual industries, Federal, State, or local government agencies, or geographic regions.
(c) Will not have significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or the ability of U.S.-based enterprises to compete with foreign-based enterprises.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) requires that agencies assess whether a rule would impose a Federal mandate that may result in the expenditure by State, local, and Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted annually for inflation) in any 1 year. As of 2025, that threshold is approximately $206 million (2024 dollars). This rule will not result in expenditures by State, local, or Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, in excess of the threshold. Thus, no written assessment of unfunded mandates is required.
Takings (
Executive Order 12630
)
This rule will not effect a taking of private property or otherwise have takings implications under
Executive Order 12630
. A takings implication assessment is not required.
Federalism (
Executive Order 13132
)
Under the criteria in section 1 of
Executive Order 13132
, this rule will not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant the preparation of a federalism summary impact statement. This rule will only affect use of federally administered lands and waters. It will have no direct effects on other areas. A federalism summary impact statement is not required.
Civil Justice Reform (
Executive Order 12988
)
This rule complies with the requirements of
Executive Order 12988
. This rule:
(a) Meets the criteria of section 3(a) requiring that all regulations be reviewed to eliminate errors and ambiguity and be written to minimize litigation; and
(b) Meets the criteria of section 3(b)(2) requiring that all regulations be written in clear language and contain clear legal standards.
Consultation With Alaska Native Tribes and Alaska Native Corporations (
Executive Order 13175
and Department Policy)
The Department of the Interior strives to strengthen its government-to-government relationship with Indian Tribes through a commitment to consultation with Indian Tribes and recognition of their right to self-governance and Tribal sovereignty. NPS staff communicated with local tribal groups regarding the VMP. The planning alternatives were developed with consideration that project actions would avoid or minimally disturb resources or values important to affiliated Alaska Native Tribes. The planning alternatives did not entail new construction or ground disturbance and are not anticipated to impede access to places of traditional religious, ceremonial, or other customary activities. NPS has evaluated this rule under the criteria in
Executive Order 13175
and under the Department's consultation policy and has determined this rule will have no substantial direct effect on Alaska Native Tribes or Alaska Native Corporation lands, water areas, or resources. However, the NPS remains available to consult with Alaska Native Tribes and Alaska Native Corporations upon request. Doyon, Limited requested consultation as part of its comments on the proposed rule. The NPS will continue to meet regularly with Doyon, Limited and engage with them on various issues related to park management, including vehicle use on the park road.
Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.)
This rule contains no new information collections. All information collections require approval under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA;
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
). The NPS may not conduct or sponsor, and you are not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA;
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
)
The NPS prepared an environmental impact statement as part of the VMP in compliance with NEPA. This rule merely conforms the regulatory text to the ROD as it has been implemented for over a decade, which identifies the limits for vehicle use that are stated in the rule. Copies of these documents are available online at
https://parkplanning.nps.gov/​dena
by clicking the link titled “Denali Park Road Vehicle Management Plan,” then the link titled “Document List.”
Effects on the Energy Supply (
Executive Order 13211
)
This rule is not a significant energy action under the definition in
Executive Order 13211
; this rule is not likely to have a significant adverse effect on the supply, distribution, or use of energy, and this rule has not otherwise been designated by the Administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs as a significant energy action. A Statement of Energy Effects in not required.

§ 13.930
Do I need a permit to operate a motor vehicle on the Denali Park road west of Savage River during the visitor season?
Yes, you must obtain a permit or other form of written authorization from the superintendent to operate a motor vehicle on the restricted section of the Denali Park road during the visitor season. No more than 160 motor vehicles may enter the restricted section of the Denali Park road per 24-hour period during the visitor season.

ACTION:
Notice of availability.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) hereby provides notice of availability of the Emissions Value Request Process in support of the U.S. Department of the Treasury's (Treasury) and Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) administration of the section 45Z Credit for Clean Fuel Production.
ADDRESSES:
The Department of Energy's section 45Z Emissions Value Request Process for use in obtaining an emissions value in support of a petition for a provisional emissions rate (PER) is located at:
https://www.energy.gov/​cmei/​45z-emissions-value-request
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Questions may be addressed to John Cabaniss at
45ZEmissionsRequest@doe.gov
or (202) 287-5531. Communication via email is preferred.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Clean Fuel Production Tax Credit (
Internal Revenue Code Section 45Z
) was established under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (
Pub. L. 117-169
), and amended by the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (
Pub. L. 119-21
). The amount of the tax credit is determined, in part, by the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions rate of the transportation fuel.
Transportation fuel producers seeking to claim the tax credit must obtain the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions rate of their transportation fuel using the applicable emissions rate table published for section 45Z, or by petitioning the Secretary of Treasury for a provisional emissions rate (PER) if the fuel's type, primary feedstock, or pathway is not included in the applicable emissions rate table. The Treasury and IRS issued notice 2025-10 (January 2025), section 45Z clean fuel production credit; request for public comments, which provided that an applicant seeking a PER must follow the latest procedures for obtaining a PER as published by the Secretary Treasury in the section 45Z regulations and in the Internal Revenue Bulletin, including the process for obtaining an emissions value from DOE that is used by the applicant to request a PER determination. On July 24, 2025, DOE published a notice of intent and request for comment regarding an Emissions Value Request process.
90 FR 34855
. On February 4, 2026, the Treasury and IRS published a notice of proposed rulemaking, which proposed the procedures that a taxpayer must follow to request a PER determination.
91 FR 5160
,
5173
.
DOE has considered the comments received regarding the Emissions Value Request Process, and is now announcing the opening of the 45Z Emissions Value Request Process.
Signing Authority
This document of the Department of Energy was signed on October 13, 2026, by Audrey Robertson, Assistant Secretary (EERE) for Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, pursuant to delegated authority from the Secretary of Energy. That document with the original signature and date is maintained by DOE. For administrative purposes only, and in compliance with requirements of the Office of the Federal Register, the undersigned DOE Federal Register Liaison Officer has been authorized to sign and submit the document in electronic format for publication, as an official document of the Department of Energy. Federal Register
.

Rule 17f-2 (
17 CFR 270.17f-2
), entitled “Custody of Investments by Registered Management Investment Company,” was adopted in 1940 under section 17(f) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 (
15 U.S.C. 80a-17(f)
) (the “Act”), and was last amended materially in 1947. Rule 17f-2 establishes safeguards for arrangements in which a registered management investment company (“fund”) is deemed to maintain custody of its own assets, such as when the fund maintains its assets in a facility that provides safekeeping but not custodial services.
[
1
]
Form N-17f-2 (
17 CFR 274.220
) is entitled “Certificate of Accounting of Securities and Similar Investments in the Custody of Management Investment Companies.” Form N-17f-2 is the cover sheet for the accountant examination certificates prepared under rule 17f-2. Form N-17f-2 facilitates the filing process for accountant examination certificates. The form has a purely administrative purpose and does not require any additional information (beyond that required by rule 17f-2) to be collected. Form N-17f-2 increases the accessibility of the examination certificates to both Commission staff and interested investors by ensuring that the certificates are filed under the proper SEC file number and correct name of a fund.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977, as amended, governs the application, processing, and disposition of petitions for modification of mandatory safety standards. Any mine operator or representative of miners may petition for an alternative method of complying with an existing safety standard. MSHA reviews the content of each submitted petition, assesses the equipment and system(s) proposed at the mine in question, and ultimately issues a decision on the petition. This notice includes a list of petitions for modification that were granted, after MSHA's review and investigation, between January 1, 2026, and June 30, 2026.
ADDRESSES:

https://www.msha.gov/​regulations/​rulemaking/​petitions-modification
.

(

petitionsformodification@dol.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Corliss A. Josephs-Conway, Acting Director, Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances, MSHA at 202-693-9440 (voice) or
petitionsformodification@dol.gov
(email). This is not a toll-free number.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
Under section 101(c) of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977, as amended, any mine operator or representative of miners may petition to use an alternative approach to comply with a mandatory safety standard. In response, the Secretary of Labor (Secretary) may modify the application of a mandatory safety standard to that mine if the Secretary determines that: (1) an alternative method exists that will guarantee no less protection for the miners affected than that provided by the standard; or (2) the application of the mandatory safety standard will result in a diminution of safety to the affected miners.
MSHA bases the final decision on the petitioner's statements, any comments and information submitted by interested persons, and a field investigation of the proposed equipment, system(s), and conditions at the mine. In some instances, MSHA may grant a petition for modification on the condition that the mine operator complies with other requirements noted in the decision. In other instances, MSHA may deny, dismiss, or revoke a petition for modification. In accordance with
30 CFR 44.5
, MSHA publishes every final action granting a petition for modification.

The Department is soliciting comments on the proposed information collection request (ICR) that is described below. The Department is especially interested in public comment addressing the following issues: (1) is the estimated burden of the data collection accurate; (2) how might the Department enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (3) how might the Department minimize the burden of this collection on the respondents, including through the use of information technology. Please note that written comments received in response to this notice will be considered public records.
Title of Collection:
High School and Beyond 2022 (HS&B:22) High School Transcript Study Data Collection.
OMB Control Number:
1850-0944.
Type of Review:
A revision of a currently approved collection.
Respondents/Affected Public:
Private Sector; State, Local, and Tribal Governments; Individuals and Households.
Total Estimated Number of Annual Responses:
13,403.
Total Estimated Number of Annual Burden Hours:
2,311.
Abstract:
The High School and Beyond Longitudinal Study of 2022 (HS&B:22) is the sixth in a series of longitudinal studies at the high school level conducted by the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), within the Institute of Education Sciences (IES) of the U.S. Department of Education. HS&B:22 is following a nationally representative sample of ninth grade students from when they started high school in the 2022-23 school year. The base-year data collection was conducted in the 2022-23 school year with ninth grade students, with a high school transcript collection planned for 2027. The original study design included a first follow-up data collection when the modal sample would have been in 12th grade. A field test was completed, but not the full-scale data collection. This request is to obtain clearance to conduct the high school transcript collection for
(
printed page 65737)
HS&B:22 sample members, which includes contacting schools and a subset of students that may not have finished at their base-year high school.
NCES encourages the public to review the materials associated with this submission on
regulations.gov
and submit comments. Part A of this submission presents information on the basic design of the HS&B:22 High School Transcript Study (HSTS) data collection. Part B discusses the statistical methods employed. Appendix A provides the communication materials that will be used for school district, school, student, and parent data collection activities.

Written comments received within two working days after the meeting will be included in the minutes. For additional information on public comment and to submit written

ACTION:
Notice and request for comment.
SUMMARY:
The OCC, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, invites comment on a continuing information collection, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA). In accordance with the requirements of the PRA, the OCC may not conduct or sponsor, and the respondent is not required to respond to, an information collection unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget (OMB) control number. The OCC is soliciting comment concerning the renewal of its information collection titled, “Conversions From Mutual to Stock Form.” The OCC also is giving notice that it has sent the collection to OMB for review.
(
printed page 65846)
DATES:
Comments must be received by November 16, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Commenters are encouraged to submit comments by email, if possible. You may submit comments by any of the following methods:
Email:
prainfo@occ.treas.gov
.
Mail:
Chief Counsel's Office, Attention: Comment Processing, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Attention: 1557-0347, 400 7th Street SW, Suite 1E-216, Washington, DC 20219.

(571) 293-4835.

You must include “OCC” as the agency name and “1557-0347” in your comment. In general, the OCC will publish comments on

et seq.
), Federal agencies must obtain approval from the OMB for each collection of information that they conduct or sponsor. “Collection of information” is defined in

and
