XI. Statutory Authority
I. Executive Summary
On April 1, 2026, the EPA established the renewable fuel volumes and percentage standards under the RFS program that apply to obligated parties for the 2026 and 2027 compliance years (“Set 2 Rule”).
[
1
]
In that final rule, the EPA reallocated a portion (70 percent) of the SREs granted or projected to be granted for 2023-2025 by including a “SRE reallocation volume” term in the equations used to calculate the RFS percentage standards under
40 CFR 80.1405
. For the 2025 compliance year, the EPA projected that SREs would result in an exempted Renewable Volume Obligation (RVO) of 990 million Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs),
[
2
]
resulting in the inclusion of approximately 700 million RINs in the 2027 SRE reallocation volume.
[
3
]
On August 31, 2026, the EPA issued decisions on 34 SRE petitions under the RFS program for the 2025 compliance year after consulting with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) and considering relevant information pursuant to Clean Air Act (CAA) section 211(o)(9).
[
4
]
The 2025 SREs granted in that action resulted in a 2025 exempted RVO of 1.76 billion RINs,
[
5
]
which is 770 million RINs greater than the volume projected in the Set 2 Rule.
[
6
]
In this action, the EPA is proposing two options for revising the SRE reallocation volumes promulgated in the Set 2 Rule to reallocate an additional 770 million RINs as a result of this significant increase in the actual 2025 exempted RVO as compared to the projected 2025 exempted RVO. This additional SRE reallocation volume represents complete (100 percent) reallocation of the additional 2025 exempted RVO (
i.e.,
the volume beyond the 990 million RINs originally projected for 2025) and aims to prevent the significantly higher-than-projected volume of 2025 SREs from reducing demand for renewable fuel and RINs in 2026 and 2027 to levels lower than anticipated in the Set 2 Rule.
This proposal describes the EPA's legal basis for considering the 2025 SREs when proposing to revise the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes, the revised SRE reallocation volumes the Agency is co-proposing for 2026 and 2027, how the statutory factors were considered, and the methodology used to calculate the co-proposed revised percentage standards for 2026 and 2027. Specifically, the EPA is co-proposing two approaches: (1) reallocate the additional 2025 exempted RVO equally between the 2026 and 2027 compliance years; and, alternatively, (2) reallocate all the additional 2025 exempted RVO to the 2027 compliance year.
Finally, the EPA notes that because the Agency is proposing to revise the existing 2026 and 2027 RFS standards under
40 CFR 80.1405(a)
, this proposed rule triggers the automatic compliance reporting deadline extension provisions under
40 CFR 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(C)
. For the 2026 compliance year, the current compliance reporting deadline is March 31, 2027. As a result of this proposed rule, and per the RFS regulations, the 2026 compliance reporting deadline will be extended to whichever of the following dates is applicable:
If the EPA finalizes the proposed revision to the 2026 RFS standards, the next quarterly reporting deadline after the date the revised 2026 RFS standards become effective.
If the EPA withdraws the proposed revision to the 2026 RFS standards, the next quarterly reporting deadline that is 60 days after the date of the Agency's withdrawal of the proposed revision to the 2026 RFS standards is published in the
Federal Register
.
If the EPA does not finalize or withdraw the proposed revision to the 2026 RFS standards within 12 months of the date of publication of this proposed rule in the
Federal Register
, the next quarterly reporting deadline that is 12 months after the date this proposed rule is published in the
Federal Register
.
For the 2027 compliance year, there is currently no established compliance reporting deadline because the EPA has not yet established the 2028 RFS standards.
[
7
]
Furthermore, the earliest the 2027 compliance reporting deadline could be is March 31, 2028, which is more than 16 months after this proposal.
[
8
]
Thus, this proposed rule is not expected to have any impact on the 2027 compliance reporting deadline.
II. Background and Policy Rationale
In the Set 2 Rule, the EPA established applicable volumes for 2026 and 2027 based on an analysis of the statutory factors and a review of implementation of the RFS program to date.
[
9
]
In doing so, the EPA determined both the volume requirements, which were intended to be met with renewable fuel produced and used in 2026 and 2027, and SRE reallocation volumes, which were intended to be met with carryover RINs attributable to the 2023-2025 SREs.
[
10
]
The 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes established in the Set 2 Rule accounted for a portion of the actual 2023 and 2024 exempted RVOs that resulted from the SRE decisions issued by the EPA in August 2025
[
11
]
and November 2025,
[
12
]
as well as a portion of the projected 2025 exempted RVO.
[
13
]
The SRE reallocation volumes correspond to three statutory categories
(
printed page 65702)
of renewable fuel (advanced biofuel, biomass-based diesel (BBD), and total renewable fuel), such that there are three SRE reallocation volumes for each year.
[
14
]
As discussed in the Set 2 Rule and elsewhere, the EPA at the time faced an unusually high backlog of pending SRE petitions for multiple compliance years resulting in an unusually material impact on overall volumes.
[
15
]
At the time of the Set 2 Rule, the EPA had issued decisions on the 2023 and 2024 SRE petitions, but not the 2025 SRE petitions. Consistent with the approach that the EPA first advanced in the 2020 RFS Rule (in which the Agency projected future exempted fuel volumes),
[
16
]
in the Set 2 Rule the Agency projected 7.55 billion gallons of exempted fuel volume in 2025 using a three-year average of the actual exempted fuel volumes from 2022-2024. This projected exempted fuel volume equaled a projected 2025 exempted RVO of 990 million RINs. The EPA reallocated 70 percent of this volume (approximately 700 million RINs) as part of the 2027 SRE reallocation volume.
[
17
]
On August 31, 2026, the EPA issued decisions on 34 SRE petitions for the 2025 compliance year after consulting with DOE and considering relevant information,
[
18
]
in which the Agency granted full (100 percent) exemptions to 18 petitions, granted partial (50 percent) exemptions to 11 petitions, denied three petitions, and determined two petitions to be ineligible.
[
19
]
The 2025 SREs resulted in a 2025 exempted fuel volume of 13.38 billion gallons, which, using the previously established percentage standards for 2025, equaled an actual 2025 exempted RVO of 1.76 billion RINs.
[
20
]
This is 770 million RINs greater than the projected 2025 exempted RVO of 990 million RINs in the Set 2 Rule.
[
21
]
In this action, the EPA is co-proposing to revise the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes to reallocate an additional 770 million RINs, which is 100 percent of the additional 2025 exempted RVO beyond the projected 2025 exempted RVO in the Set 2 Rule.
[
22
]
The actual 2025 exempted RVO was significantly higher than the volume projected by the EPA in the Set 2 Rule, resulting in an increased number of RINs available for obligated parties to use for compliance with their 2025 or future RFS obligations. These RINs represent renewable fuel produced and used in 2025 that exempt small refineries no longer need to retire for compliance because of their relieved obligations due to SREs. The availability of these RINs—and the ability for obligated parties to use them to comply with their RFS obligations in lieu of RINs generated for renewable fuel produced and used in 2026 and 2027—could reduce RIN prices and demand for renewable fuel and RINs in future years and may ultimately result in the market failing to produce the volume of renewable fuel anticipated by the volume requirements in the Set 2 Rule.
The additional 2025 exempted RVO would have impacts on the RIN market. For the 2025 compliance year, the number of RINs that need to be retired to meet the 2025 RFS obligations is 770 million RINs fewer than the EPA projected in the Set 2 Rule. While these additional RINs have no impact on the volume of renewable fuel actually produced and used in 2025 since that year is in the past, they directly increase the supply of RINs available for other obligated parties to use for compliance. As a result, obligated parties will be able to use the RFS program's carryover RIN provisions to roll these RINs forward to the 2026 compliance year and beyond.
[
23
]
The EPA expects that there may be impacts from the increased number of carryover RINs as a result of the additional 2025 exempted RVO on renewable fuel production and use in 2026 and, more acutely, in 2027. Obligated parties could choose to use these additional carryover RINs to comply with their 2026 and 2027 RFS obligations in lieu of acquiring renewable fuel produced in those years, thereby reducing the demand for renewable fuel production and use in those years. Thus, failure to mitigate the market impacts of the increased number of carryover RINs due to the additional 2025 exempted RVO could result in decreased demand for renewable fuel produced in 2026 and 2027. This magnitude of carryover RINs has the potential to depress RIN prices and decrease demand for renewable fuel in future years.
While significant quantities of carryover RINs can negatively impact the production and use of renewable fuel, carryover RINs also play an important role in providing a liquid and well-functioning RIN market, as the EPA has stated on multiple occasions.
[
24
]
The continued success of the RFS program depends on the RIN market. Carryover RINs provide obligated parties compliance flexibility for substantial uncertainties in the transportation fuel marketplace.
The EPA is co-proposing two approaches to reallocate the additional 2025 exempted RVO. Under the first approach, the EPA would reallocate the additional 2025 exempted RVO in equal amounts to both the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes.
[
25
]
This approach would result in revised 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes of similar magnitudes. In the Set 2 Rule, the EPA established 2026 and 2027 SRE
(
printed page 65703)
reallocation volumes of 0.99 and 1.04 billion RINs, respectively. Under the equal reallocation approach, the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes would each be increased by equal amounts, such that the SRE reallocation volume in each year would be approximately 1.4 billion RINs. Given the timing of this proposed rule, this approach would require obligated parties to acquire additional RINs for the 2026 compliance year after the compliance year was over.
Under the second approach, the EPA would reallocate all the additional 2025 exempted RVO to the 2027 SRE reallocation volume, as opposed to equally between 2026 and 2027.
[
26
]
This approach is consistent with the approach to SRE reallocation volumes in the Set 2 Rule, in which all the projected 2025 exempted RVO was reallocated to the 2027 SRE reallocation volume, and would ensure that all the reallocated volumes from 2025 SREs were reallocated to the same compliance year. Under the 2027 reallocation approach, the 2026 SRE reallocation volume would remain at 0.99 billion RINs, while the 2027 SRE reallocation volume would increase from 1.04 billion to 1.81 billion RINs. Reallocating all the additional 2025 exempted RVO to 2027 would provide obligated parties with additional time to prospectively adjust their compliance strategies given the increase in the 2027 SRE reallocation volume, rather than requiring obligated parties to acquire additional RINs after the compliance year was over. It would also allow the obligated parties to recover the cost of the revised 2027 SRE reallocation volume through the revenue received from the sale of obligated fuels (
i.e.,
gasoline and diesel), further limiting the impact on obligated parties.
The EPA is proposing to fully reallocate 100 percent of the additional 2025 exempted RVO because this approach would align with market expectations from the Set 2 Rule and minimize disruptions in the market as a result of the 2025 SREs. At the time the EPA promulgated the Set 2 Rule, market participants relied on the volumes promulgated in that action to inform compliance strategies, including for the 2026 and 2027 volume requirements, which require the use of specified quantities of renewable fuel in 2026 and 2027. Subsequent to the promulgation of the Set 2 Rule, the significantly higher-than-projected volume of 2025 SREs disrupted those expectations. Without additional action by the EPA, the additional 2025 exempted RVO could jeopardize the realization of the 2026 and 2027 volume requirements in the market. As described in the Set 2 Rule, the EPA designed the SRE reallocation volumes as a mechanism to require the use of RINs associated with 2023-2025 SREs, removing the ability for obligated parties to use those RINs to comply with their RFS obligations in lieu of RINs generated for renewable fuel produced and used in 2026 and 2027. Absent the SRE reallocation volumes, these RINs could reduce RIN demand and RIN prices and may ultimately result in the market failing to produce the volume of renewable fuel anticipated by the 2026 and 2027 volume requirements.
[
27
]
The EPA is therefore proposing to remedy that disruption through the required retirement of the 770 million RINs associated with the additional 2025 exempted RVO. This increases the likelihood that the 2026 and 2027 volume requirements would be realized in the market through new renewable fuel production and use rather than through the use of carryover RINs attributable to the 2025 SREs. The EPA recognizes that this approach is different from the approach to SRE reallocation volumes in the Set 2 Rule but the Agency is proposing that such change is justified for the reasons articulated in this preamble.
As noted in section IX of this preamble, the EPA is requesting comment on whether the additional SRE reallocation volumes should be different between 2026 and 2027, such as whether more or less of the additional 2025 exempted RVO should be reallocated in 2026 or 2027 (C-1).
III. Legal Justification
In this action, the EPA is co-proposing two approaches to revise the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes established in the Set 2 Rule. In doing so, the EPA is proposing to use the same authority under CAA section 211(o)(2)(B)(ii) that was used to establish the original 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes in the Set 2 Rule.
[
28
]
This section discusses that authority, as well as the EPA's authority to reconsider and revise previously established standards under the RFS program. Alternatively, the EPA may have authority under CAA section 211(o)(2)(A)(i) and (iii)(I) to “ensure” that the volumes in the Set 2 Rule are met in the market with actual renewable fuel production and use in 2026 and 2027 via a compliance mechanism.
[
29
]
The purpose of reallocating the additional 2025 exempted RVO is to prevent excess carryover RINs introduced by the 2025 SREs granted after the Set 2 Rule was finalized from removing the market incentives for actual production and use of renewable fuels in 2026 and 2027 at the volumes anticipated by the Set 2 Rule. As noted in section IX of this preamble, the EPA is requesting comment on the Agency's legal authority to reallocate the additional 2025 exempted RVO (C-2), including under CAA section 211(o)(2)(A)(i).
A. Legal Authority for SRE Reallocation Volumes
As in the Set 2 Rule, the EPA is co-proposing to revise the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes utilizing the “set authority” in CAA section 211(o)(2)(B)(ii), which directs the Agency to “set,” or establish, applicable volumes of renewable fuel for use as transportation fuel in the U.S. for years after those specified in the statutory tables. Under that provision, the Administrator shall, in coordination with the Secretary of Agriculture and Secretary of Energy, determine the applicable volume of each renewable fuel category based on a review of implementation of the RFS program and an analysis of statutory factors. Congress provided the EPA flexibility by enumerating factors that the Administrator must consider without mandating particular forms of analysis or specifying how the Administrator must weigh the various factors against one another. Thus, as the CAA “does not state what weight should be accorded to the relevant factors,” it “give[s] EPA considerable discretion to weigh and balance the various factors required by statute.”
[
30
]
There are also prescriptive requirements for specific fuel categories in CAA section 211(o)(2)(B)(iii)-(v).
The EPA is proposing to use this authority to consider the 2025 SREs and revise the existing SRE reallocation volumes to incorporate the additional 2025 exempted RVO. In discussing the statutory conditions in CAA section 211(o)(2)(B)(iii) and (v) in the Set 2 Rule, the EPA assessed the total applicable volumes, including the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes.
(
printed page 65704)
Because this proposed rule would increase the SRE reallocation volumes for individual renewable fuel categories in proportionate amounts (
i.e.,
a proportionate increase in the BBD, advanced biofuel, and total renewable fuel standards), the EPA points to the discussion of these conditions in the Set 2 Rule, which all remain applicable to the Agency's proposed action here.
[
31
]
B. Considerations in Revising Established SRE Reallocation Volumes and for Timing of This Action
The EPA generally has authority to reconsider and revise the Agency's rulemakings, unless provided otherwise by statute, so long as we use the same procedures to amend a rule as we used to promulgate it in the first instance and set forth good reasons for the reconsideration.
[
32
]
The EPA's authority to revise RFS standards specifically is further buttressed by the statutory structure, under which Congress created a prospective regulatory scheme
[
33
]
that expressly contemplates the possibility of adjustments based on unanticipated circumstances.
[
34
]
This understanding of the EPA's authority is longstanding; the Agency previously revised the 2011, 2013, and 2020 annual rules and has also adjudicated on the merits numerous petitions to revise other annual rules.
[
35
]
The EPA believes the power to reconsider, as with the power to promulgate a rule in the first instance, remains extant even if the rule operates retroactively or is promulgated after the statutory deadline, so long as the Agency reasonably considers and mitigates the burdens associated with a retroactive or delayed rulemaking as described in this section.
The 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes, established under CAA section 211(o)(2)(B)(ii) as a component of the applicable volumes for 2026 and 2027, are similar to the revisions to the volume requirements promulgated in the EPA's prior actions. CAA section 211(o)(2)(B)(i) contains the statutory volumes, which can then be modified using the EPA's waiver authorities. Likewise, CAA section 211(o)(2)(B)(ii) requires the EPA to set volumes after 2022, which can also be modified using the Agency's waiver authorities and reconsidered, as appropriate, to the extent justified by relevant factors.
[
36
]
The Agency acknowledges that reconsideration can negatively impact regulatory certainty and disrupt market expectations created by previously promulgated standards. This may especially be the case if the effects of reconsideration are retroactive, and such retroactive rules must consider and mitigate burdens on obligated parties, as discussed further below. Moreover, in the Set 2 Rule, the EPA expressly stated that the Agency did not intend, at that time, to revisit that rulemaking and subsequently adjust the standards.
[
37
]
Although the EPA expects that any reliance interests obligated parties had in the percentage standards from the Set 2 Rule would be outweighed by the considerations informing this proposal (
i.e.,
the proposed attempt to maintain the volumes from the Set 2 Rule in light of the recent 2025 SREs), as noted in section IX of this preamble, the Agency is requesting comment on reliance interests to better inform our decision-making on this topic (C-3).
At the same time, reconsideration can also address the impacts of unexpected actions and market disruptions that occur after the standards have been set and that, if not accounted for, could lead to reduced demand for renewable fuel. In this action, the EPA is co-proposing to revise the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes in response to an unanticipated event—the significantly higher-than-projected volume of 2025 SREs—that has occurred since the promulgation of the Set 2 Rule and that could have direct and significant impacts on the fuels market. The EPA believes this event has created an unusual situation in which retroactive reconsideration and revision of the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes are warranted.
In the Set 2 Rule, the EPA attempted to account for the exempted RVOs associated with 2023-2025 SREs through the establishment of SRE reallocation volumes, which included a projection of the 2025 exempted RVO that was reallocated to the 2027 compliance year. The projected 2025 exempted RVO, however, fell short of the actual 2025 exempted RVO by a sizeable margin. As described in section II of this preamble, the significantly higher-than-projected volume of 2025 SREs resulted in an additional 770 million RINs becoming available for compliance with the 2025 and later compliance years. Consistent with the EPA's justification for establishing the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes in the Set 2 Rule, these excess RINs could result in decreased demand in future years for RINs and renewable fuel, as well as decreased RIN prices, and may ultimately result in the market failing to produce the volume of renewable fuel anticipated by the volume requirements established in the Set 2 Rule. This is because, through the use of the RFS program's carryover RIN provisions, the additional 2025 exempted RVO would allow obligated parties to effectively use an additional 770 million RINs from the 2025 compliance year to comply with their 2026 and 2027 RFS obligations in lieu of RINs generated for renewable fuel produced and used in 2026 and 2027.
The EPA recognizes that in co-proposing to revise the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes, the Agency is doing so after the statutory deadlines for the 2026 and 2027 standards of October 31, 2024, and October 31, 2025, respectively.
[
38
]
The EPA also recognizes that if this rule is finalized in 2026, it will be partially retroactive for the 2026 compliance year, and if it is finalized in 2027, it will be fully retroactive for the 2026 compliance year and partially retroactive for the 2027 compliance year. Additionally, barring unusual circumstances, the EPA believes it is generally appropriate to avoid reconsidering and revising previously finalized RFS standards.
[
39
]
Nonetheless, the EPA is proposing to do so for 2026 and 2027 because the Agency has determined that unanticipated events have occurred that affect fuel markets
(
printed page 65705)
and consequently affect renewable fuel demand. The EPA additionally finds that the burden of such a standard is materially mitigated by the fact that the Agency intends for the co-proposed revised SRE reallocation volumes to be met using carryover RINs attributable to the 2025 SREs, which will be available in greater numbers than anticipated when the Agency established the 2026 and 2027 standards due to the significantly higher-than-projected volume of 2025 SREs.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit held that the EPA retains authority to promulgate volumes and annual standards beyond the statutory deadlines, even those that apply retroactively, so long as the Agency exercises our authority “reasonably.”
[
40
]
In doing so, the EPA must balance the burden on obligated parties of a delayed rulemaking with the broader goal of the RFS program to increase renewable fuel use.
[
41
]
The D.C. Circuit noted reasonableness includes “whether obligated parties had adequate lead time and access to a sufficient number of RINs to comply with the delayed requirement.”
[
42
]
In upholding the EPA's late and retroactive standards in
ACE,
the D.C. Circuit considered several specific factors, including the availability of RINs for compliance, the amount of lead time and adequate notice for obligated parties, and the availability of compliance flexibilities.
[
43
]
In addressing rulemakings that were late (
i.e.,
those issued after the statutory deadline) but not retroactive, the D.C. Circuit emphasized the amount of lead time and adequate notice for obligated parties.
[
44
]
In 2015, the EPA established the BBD volume requirements for 2014-2017 and missed the statutory deadline—that the Agency establish an applicable volume target for BBD no later than 14 months before the first year to which that volume requirement will apply—for all four years.
[
45
]
The D.C. Circuit found that the EPA properly balanced the relevant considerations and had provided sufficient notice to parties in establishing the applicable volume requirements for 2014-2017.
[
46
]
The D.C. Circuit, in a later case, noted its repeated holdings that the “EPA may promulgate late, and even retroactive, volume requirements so long as it `reasonably considers and mitigates any hardship caused to obligated parties by reason of the lateness.' ”
[
47
]
In so holding, the D.C. Circuit noted the EPA's explanation of the achievability of the RFS standards, the timing of compliance demonstrations in relation to the final rule, and existing flexibilities in the RFS program for obligated parties.
[
48
]
As described in section I of this preamble, this action triggers the automatic compliance reporting deadline extension provisions under
40 CFR 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(C)
. For the 2026 compliance year, obligated parties will have at least five months after this proposed rule is published in the
Federal Register
before they have to demonstrate compliance with their 2026 RFS obligations by the current 2026 compliance reporting deadline of March 31, 2027, and could have additional time for compliance (
e.g.,
until June 1, 2027) depending on when the EPA finalizes any of these proposed changes. While the 2027 compliance reporting deadline will not be determined until the EPA establishes the 2028 RFS standards, the deadline can be no earlier than March 31, 2028, which is over 16 months after this proposal.
[
49
]
This proposed rule also provides notice to obligated parties that their RFS obligations for 2026 and 2027 may be increasing. It is possible that the revised 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes will be partly or fully retroactive, depending on the timing of the final rulemaking and the approach that the EPA finalizes. Under either approach, there are concerns with notice and potential retroactive effects if this rule is finalized in 2027, though obligated parties are on notice in advance of 2027 for the potential adjustments to the 2027 SRE reallocation volume under either co-proposed approach. If the equal reallocation approach is adopted, notice for the revised 2026 SRE reallocation volume would primarily amount to this proposed rule, provided in late 2026.
[
50
]
The EPA will endeavor to work quickly to minimize retroactive effects of this action and will also consider these issues in determining the Agency's final approach.
RIN acquisition to comply with revised 2026 standards would likely occur late in the compliance year, or even after the compliance year is over, resulting in obligated parties retroactively adjusting compliance strategies as compared to the 2027 reallocation approach. Under the 2027 reallocation approach, an increased obligation in 2027 only would give obligated parties notice of the revised 2027 standards prior to the 2027 compliance year so that those parties would have advanced notice of their increased obligations and limit the retroactive effects of the revised 2027 SRE reallocation volume.
Because the EPA anticipates that the 770 million RINs associated with the additional 2025 exempted RVO will be available in the market as carryover RINs, obligated parties should be able to acquire the necessary RINs prior to demonstrating compliance with their 2026 and 2027 RFS obligations. The EPA anticipates that additional information will be available at the time of the final rulemaking; the Agency plans to further assess the feasibility and market impacts of the revised SRE reallocation volumes at that time. While this proposed rule would require a drawdown in the number of carryover RINs available, additional carryover RINs should remain available for obligated parties given the EPA's prior action in the Set 2 Rule to reallocate less than the full amount of the 2023-2025 exempted RVOs. Additionally, obligated parties would continue to have the ability to use existing compliance flexibilities to comply with the revised SRE reallocation volumes, including carrying forward a deficit from one compliance year into the next.
IV. Co-Proposed Revised SRE Reallocation Volumes
As described in section II of this preamble, the EPA is co-proposing two approaches to revise the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes. Both approaches would increase the total 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes by 770 million RINs, which is equivalent to 100 percent of the additional 2025 exempted RVO beyond the projected 2025 exempted RVO of 990 million RINs from the Set 2 Rule. Under the equal reallocation approach, the additional 770 million RINs would be reallocated equally between the 2026 and 2027 compliance years. Under the 2027 reallocation approach, the additional 770 million RINs would be reallocated only to the 2027 compliance year, and no changes would be made to

The EPA is not reopening the analyses supporting the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes established in the Set 2 Rule, which the Agency established prospectively as a mechanism to preserve the stringency of the 2026 and 2027 volume requirements. The updated analysis provided here in support of the proposed revision represents a supplemental analysis to the determinations made in the Set 2 Rule that the EPA is not reopening. VI. Statutory Factor Analysis
The EPA considered the statutory factors specified in CAA section 211(o)(2)(B)(ii) in establishing the renewable fuel volumes and percentage standards for 2025 in the Set 1 Rule
[
54
]
and for 2026 and 2027 in the Set 2 Rule. In light of the significantly higher-than-projected volume of 2025 SREs, the purpose of this proposed rule is to account for the difference between the projected 2025 exempted RVO in the Set 2 Rule and the actual 2025 exempted RVO. Absent this action, the significantly higher-than-projected volume of 2025 SREs could significantly increase the number of carryover RINs available for use in 2026 and 2027,
(
printed page 65707)
which could in turn reduce RIN prices and demand for RINs and renewable fuel in those years. This could also affect some of the statutory factors, including the expected annual rate of future commercial production of renewable fuels, as discussed further below.
The EPA acknowledges that neither this action nor the 2025 SREs will affect the volume of renewable fuel produced or consumed in the U.S. in 2025, and that any effect these decisions may have on renewable fuel production and use in 2026 is limited. Instead, the significantly higher-than-projected volume of 2025 SREs will result in fewer RINs being retired for compliance in 2025 and, all else being equal, a higher number of carryover RINs being available for use in 2026 and future years. Increased numbers of carryover RINs can negatively impact the demand for RINs and renewable fuel. This is because obligated parties can use carryover RINs to meet their compliance obligations in 2026 and 2027 in lieu of acquiring RINs generated for renewable fuel produced and used in these years. An increase in the availability of carryover RINs to meet obligated parties' 2026 and 2027 RFS obligations could decrease the demand for current-year RINs. The co-proposed revised SRE reallocation volumes are intended to prevent increased numbers of carryover RINs from decreasing demand for renewable fuel below the volumes established for 2026 and 2027 in the Set 2 Rule.
The EPA is co-proposing revised 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes as part of setting overall RFS applicable volumes pursuant to the Agency's authority in CAA section 211(o)(2)(B)(ii). As discussed in section III.A of this preamble, the CAA requires that renewable fuel volumes established using this authority are based on a review of implementation of the program and an analysis of statutory factors.
The EPA is considering the significantly higher-than-projected volume of 2025 SREs under the Agency's directive to review the implementation of the program. These exemptions have a direct impact on the RFS obligations both for the exempted small refineries (which now have reduced or zero RFS obligations) and for all obligated parties in aggregate (which can now carry over a greater number of carryover RINs into the 2026 and later compliance years). Further, because obligated parties can now use the carryover RINs that otherwise would have been retired for compliance but for the 2025 SREs, exemptions granted in one year can have an impact on the demand for RINs and renewable fuel in future years.
The EPA has also considered the statutory factors specified in CAA section 211(o)(2)(B)(ii) in co-proposing the revised 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes. The EPA projects that the portion of the RFS obligations represented by the co-proposed revised SRE reallocation volumes would be met with carryover RINs attributable to the 2025 SREs. The EPA therefore does not expect that this action will increase the production and use of renewable fuel beyond the volumes previously established for 2026 and 2027 (24.02 billion RINs and 24.46 billion RINs, respectively). Conversely, if the EPA does not account for the additional 2025 exempted RVO, the increase in available carryover RINs resulting from the 2025 SREs could result in lower commercial production of renewable fuel in 2026 and 2027 than intended when establishing the required volumes for these years in the Set 2 Rule.
In general, the statutory factors that the EPA must consider when establishing the applicable volumes for years after 2022 are impacted by the production and use of renewable fuel and are not impacted by the use of carryover RINs. Increased production of renewable fuel is expected to have impacts on “air quality, climate change, conversion of wetlands, ecosystems, wildlife habitat, water quality, and water supply,” “energy security,” “infrastructure,” “job creation, the price and supply of agricultural commodities, rural economic development, and food prices,” among other factors.
[
55
]
The use of carryover RINs to satisfy RFS obligations is not expected to impact these factors. Given this proposed rule's purpose in maintaining the volumes established for 2026 and 2027 in the Set 2 Rule, the EPA has also considered the impact on the expected annual rate of future commercial production of renewable fuels.
[
56
]
The EPA intends that this proposed rule, if finalized, would not result in an impact on the expected annual rate of future commercial production of renewable fuels in 2026 and 2027.
This proposed rule is intended to account for the anticipated market impacts of the additional 2025 exempted RVO rather than to propose changes that would result in higher (or lower) volumes of renewable fuel than previously established for 2026 and 2027. In the Set 2 Rule, the EPA analyzed the impact of the volume requirements for 2026 and 2027 in relation to the No RFS Baseline.
[
57
]
The EPA believes this analysis remains proper, as this proposed rule seeks to maintain the production and use of renewable fuel volumes in the Set 2 Rule. The EPA has therefore largely not revised the Agency's analysis of the impact of the renewable fuel volumes for 2026 and 2027 on the statutory factors presented in the Set 2 Rule and the Set 2 Rule RIA, as we do not project that this proposed rule would result in renewable fuel production and use in 2026 and 2027 that differs materially from the volumes previously analyzed.
The co-proposed revised SRE reallocation volumes would result in higher percentage standards for obligated parties than would otherwise be the case, which in turn would require obligated parties to acquire greater quantities of RINs to retire for compliance. The EPA projects that, in aggregate, obligated parties would acquire these additional RINs by purchasing carryover RINs from other parties rather than blending additional quantities of renewable fuel. Because the EPA does not expect this action to result in an increase in the production and use of renewable fuel, the Agency does not anticipate impacts on most statutory factors.
The one statutory factor that the EPA does project would be impacted by this proposed rule is the impact of the use of renewable fuels on the cost to consumers of transportation fuel and on the cost to transport goods. The EPA does expect that, on average at the national level, obligated parties would likely pass on the costs of purchasing these additional RINs to consumers, and that this proposed rule could increase the cost of transportation fuel to consumers. The EPA's assessment of the impacts of this proposed rule on fuel prices are shown in Table VI-1.

VIII. Severability
If finalized, the EPA intends for the revised 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes to be severable from the remainder of the 2026 and 2027 volume requirements. The EPA's justification for each volume is independent, such that invalidation of the SRE reallocation volumes would not impact the Agency's estimates of renewable fuel that are associated with new renewable fuel production in the market in 2026 and 2027. The EPA's justification for the revised SRE reallocation volumes is independent of that establishing the 2026 and 2027 volume requirements in the Set 2 Rule, even though the two terms are additive. The EPA does not believe that it would be appropriate to further delay implementation of the 2026 and 2027 volume requirements if a court were to find defects in the revised SRE reallocation volumes.
The EPA also intends for the revised SRE reallocation volumes to be severable from each of the technical corrections in section VII of this preamble, as each is independently justified and each function separately from the others.

D. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
I certify that this action will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the RFA. The small entities directly regulated by the annual percentage standards associated with the RFS volumes are small refiners that produce gasoline or diesel fuel, which are defined at
13 CFR 121.201
. The EPA believes that there are currently six refiners (owning seven refineries) producing gasoline and/or diesel that meet the definition of small entity by having 1,500 employees or fewer. To evaluate the impacts of the co-proposed revised SRE reallocation volumes on small entities, the EPA has conducted a screening analysis to assess whether the Agency should make a finding that this action will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
[
59
]
This action does not change the compliance flexibilities currently offered to small entities under the RFS program and currently available information shows that the impact on small entities from implementation of this rule will not be significant. The EPA has reviewed and assessed the available information, which shows that obligated parties, in general on a nationwide scale, are able to recover the cost of acquiring the RINs necessary for compliance with the RFS standards through higher sales prices of the petroleum products they sell than would be expected in the absence of the RFS program.
[
60
]
This is true whether obligated parties acquire RINs by purchasing renewable fuel with attached RINs or purchasing separated RINs. The costs of the RFS program are thus being passed on to consumers in a highly competitive marketplace. Even if the EPA were to assume that the cost of acquiring RINs was not recovered by obligated parties, a cost-to-sales ratio test shows that the costs to small entities of the co-proposed revised RFS standards in this action are less than one percent of the value of their sales.
[
61
]
While the screening analysis described above supports a certification that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on small refiners, the EPA continues to believe that it is more appropriate to consider the 2026 and 2027 standards as a part of the Agency's ongoing implementation of the overall RFS program. When considered this way, the impacts of the RFS program as a whole on small entities were addressed in the RFS2 Rule, which was the rule that implemented the entire program as required by the Energy Independence and Security Act (EISA) of 2007.
[
62
]
As such, the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA) panel process that took place prior to the RFS2 Rule was also for the entire RFS program and looked at impacts on small refiners through the full implementation of the statutory volume targets, which continue to exceed the volumes proposed in this action.
For the SBREFA process for the RFS2 Rule, the EPA analyzed the potential impacts of the RFS regulations on small entities. As a part of this analysis, the EPA convened a Small Business Advocacy Review (SBAR) Panel (“the Panel”). During the Panel process, the EPA gathered information and recommendations from Small Entity Representatives (SERs) on how to reduce the impact of the rule on small entities, and those comments are detailed in the Final Panel Report.
[
63
]
The EPA also conducted an analysis of the potential impacts of the RFS program on all refiners, including small refiners, and found that the program would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
[
64
]
For small refiners subject to the RFS program, the analysis included a cost-to-sales ratio test, a ratio of the estimated annualized compliance costs to the value of sales per company. From this test, the EPA estimated that all directly regulated small entities would have compliance costs less than one percent of their sales over the full implementation of the statutory volume targets.
[
65
]
Furthermore, the EPA conducted a section 610 review of the RFS program in May 2020, in which the Agency was required to determine whether the RFS program should continue without change or should be rescinded or amended, consistent with the stated objectives of the CAA, to minimize any significant economic impact of the rule upon a substantial
(
printed page 65710)
number of small entities.
[
66
]
Following a review of relevant evidence, the EPA did not identify any such potential changes that would reduce burden on a substantial number of small entities in a manner consistent with the stated objectives of the CAA or EISA and concluded that no changes to the RFS program were warranted.
[
67
]
The EPA has determined that this action will not impose any additional requirements on small entities beyond those already analyzed, since the impacts of this rule are not greater or fundamentally different than those already considered in the analysis for the RFS2 Rule assuming full implementation of the statutory volume targets. While in this action the EPA is co-proposing to revise the 2026 and 2027 SRE reallocation volumes through the Agency's authority in CAA section 211(o)(2)(B)(ii) rather than reducing the statutory volumes through our waiver authorities (as was the case through 2022), the magnitude of the co-proposed revised advanced biofuel and total renewable fuel applicable volumes in this action nonetheless remain significantly below the statutory volume targets analyzed in the RFS2 Rule.
[
68
]
Compared to the burden that would be imposed under the volumes that the EPA assessed in the analysis for the RFS2 Rule (
i.e.,
the volumes specified in the CAA), the volumes in this action would reduce burden on small entities. Regarding the BBD standard, it is a nested standard within the advanced biofuel category and, as discussed in the Set 2 Rule, the BBD applicable volumes for 2026 and 2027 are below the volume of BBD that is anticipated to be produced and used to satisfy the advanced biofuel and total renewable fuel requirements.
[
69
]
In other words, the volume of BBD actually used in 2026 and 2027 will be driven not by the 2026 and 2027 BBD standards, but rather by the 2026 and 2027 advanced biofuel and total renewable fuel standards. The net result of the revised volumes being co-proposed in this action is a reduction in burden as compared to implementation of the statutory volume targets assumed in the RFS2 Rule analysis.
Furthermore, to the degree that small entities may be impacted by this action, these impacts are mitigated by the existing compliance flexibilities in the RFS program that are available to small entities, which the EPA is not proposing to change in this rule. These flexibilities include being able to comply through RIN trading rather than renewable fuel blending, 20 percent RIN rollover allowance (
i.e.,
up to 20 percent of an obligated party's RVO can be met using previous-year RINs), and deficit carry-forward (
i.e.,
the ability to carry over a deficit from a given year into the following year, provided that the deficit is satisfied together with the next year's RVO). Additionally, as required by CAA section 211(o)(9)(B), the RFS regulations include a hardship relief provision that allows for a small refinery to petition for an extension of its small refinery exemption at any time based on a showing that the refinery is experiencing a “disproportionate economic hardship.”
[
70
]
The RFS regulations provide the same relief to small refiners that are not eligible for small refinery relief.
[
71
]
In the RFS2 Rule, the EPA discussed other potential small entity flexibilities that had been suggested by the Panel or through comments, but the Agency did not adopt them, in part because we had serious concerns regarding our legal authority to do so.
[
72
]
In sum, this rule would not change the compliance flexibilities currently offered to small entities under the RFS program and available information shows that the impact on small entities from implementation of this rule would not be significant. The EPA has therefore concluded that this action will not have any significant adverse economic impact on directly regulated small entities.

                         CAA section 211(o)(5) requires that the EPA establish a credit program as part of the Agency's RFS regulations and that the credits be valid for obligated parties to show compliance for 12 months after the date of generation.

Obligated parties can obtain more RINs than needed in a given compliance year, allowing them to carry over these RINs for use in the subsequent compliance year, although the RFS regulations limit the use of these carryover RINs to 20 percent of the obligated party's RVO. For the total number of available carryover RINs to be preserved from one year to the next, individual carryover RINs are used for compliance before they expire and are replaced with newer vintage RINs that are then held for use in the next year. For example, 2025 carryover RINs must be used for compliance in 2026 or they will expire. AGENCY:
Mine Safety and Health Administration, Department of Labor.
ACTION:
Proposed rule; reopening of comment period and notice of public hearing.
SUMMARY:
In response to a public request, the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) is reopening the rulemaking record and is scheduling a virtual public hearing on the Agency's proposed rule published on July 1, 2025, titled, “
Powered Air Purifying Respirators (PAPRs) in Underground Mines
.”
DATES:
Reopening of the comment period:
MSHA is reopening the comment period for the proposed rule published on July 1, 2025, (
90 FR 28406
) for additional public comments. All new comments must be received or postmarked by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on December 8, 2026.
Public Hearing:
The virtual public hearing will be held on November 17, 2026. Information on how to participate is listed below under
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments and informational materials, identified by Docket No. MSHA-2025-0089, electronically at
https://www.regulations.gov
. Follow the online instructions for making electronic submissions. You should not include personal or proprietary information that you do not wish to disclose publicly. If you mark parts of a comment as “business confidential” information, MSHA will not post those parts of the comment. Otherwise, MSHA will post all comments without change, including any personal information provided. MSHA cautions against submitting personal information. Interested parties may present verbal testimony at the virtual public hearing. For more information on the public hearing, see
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Corliss A. Josephs-Conway, Acting Director, Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances, MSHA at 202-693-9440 (voice). This is not a toll-free number.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
On July 1, 2025, MSHA published the proposed rule, “
Powered Air Purifying Respirators (PAPRs) in Underground Mines
” (
90 FR 28406
). The proposed rule would allow non-permissible PAPRs that have not been evaluated and approved by MSHA using the
30 CFR part 18
requirements to be used in specified underground areas of gassy mines. The proposed rule would also establish requirements for the features and maintenance of non-permissible PAPRs and the mining conditions where non-permissible PAPRs can be used. The proposed rule opened a 30-day public comment period, that was extended an additional 30 days, until September 2, 2025 (
90 FR 34405
). During the comment period, MSHA received a request for a public hearing on the proposed rule. MSHA is reopening the comment period for the proposed rule and announcing a virtual public hearing to allow industry, labor, and other interested parties an additional opportunity to present oral statements, written comments, and other information on the proposed rule.
II. Virtual Public Hearing
MSHA will hold a fully virtual public hearing to accept comments from the public on the proposed rule, “
Powered Air Purifying Respirators (PAPRs) in Underground Mines
” (
90 FR 28406
), on November 17, 2026. The event will begin at 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time and will end after the last presenter speaks.
Date and time
Virtual meeting access
Contact No.
November 17, 2026, 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time
Virtual meeting accessible online at:
https://www.msha.gov/​regulations/​
rulemaking/paprs-public-hearing
.
202-693-9440
The virtual public hearing will begin with an opening statement from MSHA, followed by an opportunity for members of the public to make oral presentations. Speakers and other attendees may present information to MSHA for inclusion in the rulemaking record. The hearing will be conducted in an informal manner. Formal rules of evidence and cross examination will not apply.
Those who wish to speak during the virtual public hearing are asked to register at:
https://www.msha.gov/​regulations/​rulemaking/​paprs-public-hearing
. Speakers should register by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on November 13, 2026. If you do not register in advance and you wish to speak, you will be called after all those who registered have spoken.
A verbatim transcript of the hearing will be prepared and made a part of the rulemaking record. A copy of the transcript will be available to the public. MSHA will make the transcript available at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
III. Request for Comments
MSHA is interested in receiving comments from all members of the mining community and all interested stakeholders. MSHA will accept comments from any interested party, including those not presenting oral statements during the virtual public hearing. Where possible, specific examples to support a commenter's rationale are strongly encouraged.
MSHA will accept post-hearing written comments and other appropriate information for the rulemaking record from any interested party, including those not presenting oral statements, received by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on December 8, 2026. Comments previously submitted on the proposed
(
printed page 65698)
rule do not need to be resubmitted and will be fully considered in development of the final rule.

SUMMARY:
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is announcing an opportunity for the public to comment on CMS' intention to collect information from the public. Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), federal agencies are required to publish notice in the
Federal Register
concerning each proposed collection of information (including each proposed extension or reinstatement of an existing collection of information) and to allow 60 days for public comment on the proposed action. Interested persons are invited to send comments regarding our burden estimates or any other aspect of this collection of information, including the necessity and utility of the proposed information collection for the proper performance of the agency's functions, the accuracy of the estimated burden, ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected, and the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology to minimize the information collection burden.
DATES:

ADDRESSES:

1.

http://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the instructions for “Comment or Submission” or “More Search Options” to find the information collection document(s) that are accepting comments.

Contents
This notice sets out a summary of the use and burden associated with the following information collections. More detailed information can be found in each collection's supporting statement and associated materials (see
ADDRESSES
).
Under the PRA (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
), federal agencies must obtain approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for each collection of information they conduct or sponsor. The term “collection of information” is defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(3)
and
5 CFR 1320.3(c)
and includes agency requests or requirements that members of the public submit reports, keep records, or provide information to a third party. Section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA requires federal agencies to publish a 60-day notice in the
Federal Register
concerning each proposed collection of information, including each proposed extension or reinstatement of an existing collection of information, before submitting the collection to OMB for approval. To comply with this requirement, CMS is publishing this notice.
Information Collections
1.
Type of Information Collection Request:

Title of Information Collection:
Annual State Report on CMS Value Based Purchasing Arrangements (VBP) Supplemental Rebate Agreements;
Use:
The Affordable Care Act created Health Insurance Exchanges (Exchanges), marketplaces where consumers and small businesses can purchase private health insurance. Consumers who access health insurance coverage through Exchanges can receive skilled assistance from Navigators and certified application counselors (CACs) who provide information and help facilitate enrollment in qualified health plans (QHPs) and determine whether consumers potentially qualify for insurance affordability programs through an Exchange. Exchanges will use the information collected to certify individual Navigators, Certified Application Counselors (CACs), or certified application counselor designated organization (CDOs) and to maintain CMS records related to those certifications and designations. CDOs will use the information collected to manage their internal processes to certify individual CACs. Exchanges will also use the information collected to inform the public about the availability of application services from Navigators and CACs.

2.
Type of Information Collection Request:
Revision of a currently approved collection;
Title of Information Collection:
Generic Clearance for Improving Customer Experience (OMB Circular A-11, Section 280 Implementation);
Use:
(
printed page 65748)
Whether seeking a loan, Social Security benefits, veterans benefits, or other services provided by the Federal Government, individuals and businesses expect Government customer services to be efficient and intuitive, just like services from leading private-sector organizations. Yet the 2016 American Consumer Satisfaction Index and the 2017 Forrester Federal Customer Experience Index show that, on average, Government services lag nine percentage points behind the private sector.
A modern, streamlined and responsive customer experience means: raising government-wide customer experience to the average of the private sector service industry; developing indicators for high-impact Federal programs to monitor progress towards excellent customer experience and mature digital services; and providing the structure (including increasing transparency) and resources to ensure customer experience is a focal point for agency leadership. To support this, OMB Circular A-11 Section 280 established government-wide standards for mature customer experience organizations in government and measurement. To enable Federal programs to deliver the experience taxpayers deserve, they must undertake three general categories of activities: conduct ongoing customer research, gather and share customer feedback, and test services and digital products.
These data collection efforts may be either qualitative or quantitative in nature or may consist of mixed methods. Additionally, data may be collected via a variety of means, including but not limited to electronic or social media, direct or indirect observation (
i.e.,
in person, video and audio collections), interviews, questionnaires, surveys, and focus groups. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) will limit its inquiries to data collections that solicit strictly voluntary opinions or responses. Steps will be taken to ensure anonymity of respondents in each activity covered by this request.
The results of the data collected will be used to improve the delivery of Federal services and programs. It will include the creation of personas, customer journey maps, and reports and summaries of customer feedback data and user insights. It will also provide government-wide data on customer experience that can be displayed on
performance.gov
to help build transparency and accountability of Federal programs to the customers they serve.
CMS will collect this information by electronic means when possible, as well as by mail, fax, telephone, technical discussions, and in-person interviews. CMS may also utilize observational techniques to collect this information.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is announcing an opportunity for the public to comment on CMS' intention to collect information from the public. Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), federal agencies are required to publish notice in the
Federal Register
concerning each proposed collection of information (including each proposed extension or reinstatement of an existing collection of information) and to allow 60 days for public comment on the proposed action. Interested persons are invited to send comments regarding our burden estimates or any other aspect of this collection of information, including the necessity and utility of the proposed information collection for the proper performance of the agency's functions, the accuracy of the estimated burden, ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected, and the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology to minimize the information collection burden.

When commenting, please reference the document identifier or OMB control number. To be assured consideration, comments and recommendations must be submitted in any one of the following ways:

http://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the instructions for “Comment or Submission” or “More Search Options” to find the information collection document(s) that are accepting comments.
2.
By regular mail.
You may mail written comments to the following address: CMS, Office of Strategic Operations and Regulatory Affairs, Division of Regulations Development, Attention: Document Identifier: CMS-10143/OMB Control Number: 0938-0958, Room C4-26-05, 7500 Security Boulevard, Baltimore, Maryland 21244-1850.

William N. Parham at (410) 786-4669.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Contents
This notice sets out a summary of the use and burden associated with the following information collection. More detailed information can be found in the collection's supporting statement and associated materials (see
ADDRESSES
).
Under the PRA (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
), federal agencies must obtain approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for each collection of information they conduct or sponsor. The term “collection of information” is defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(3)
and
5 CFR 1320.3(c)
and includes agency requests or requirements that members of the public submit reports, keep records, or provide information to a third party. Section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA requires federal agencies to publish a 60-day notice in the
Federal Register
concerning each proposed collection of information, including each proposed extension or reinstatement of an existing collection of information, before submitting the collection to OMB for approval. To comply with this requirement, CMS is publishing this notice.
Information Collections
1.
Type of Information Collection Request:
Revision of a currently approved collection;
Title of Information Collection:
State Data for the Medicare Modernization Act (MMA)
; Use:
The Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 (
Public Law 108-173
) requires CMS to calculate the payment rates for the Phased-Down State Contribution (PDSC) for Part D each year using the latest available National Health Expenditure (NHE) estimates of per capita drug expenditure growth for the period 2003 to 2006, combined with the annual percentage increase (API) in average per capita aggregate Part D expenditures for 2007 and later years, as defined in section 1860D-2(b)(6) of the Social Security Act.
Section 103(a)(2) of the MMA addresses the PDSC process for the Medicare program. The PDSC is a partial recoupment from the states of ongoing Medicaid drug costs for dually eligible beneficiaries assumed by Medicare under the MMA, which (absent the MMA) would have been paid for by the states.
As CMS leverages MMA data on dual eligibility status into systems supporting all four parts of the Medicare program (which includes Original Medicare, Medicare Advantage, and Part D), it is important that dual eligibility status is accurate and up to date. Dual eligibility status can change at any time in a month. Daily status updates mitigate the risk of a lack of access to the correct level of benefit at the correct level of payment. Daily data exchange is critical to timely access to affordable benefits; without daily exchanges, CMS would experience a lag in its ability to automatically enroll these individuals in Medicare drug plans or deem them automatically eligible for the low-income subsidy for Part D premiums, deductibles, and copayments.
Since 2005, states have been submitting files at least monthly to CMS to identify all dually eligible beneficiaries. This includes full-benefit dually eligible beneficiaries and partial-benefit dually eligible beneficiaries (
i.e.,
those who get Medicaid help with Medicare premiums, and often for cost-sharing but are not otherwise eligible for Medicaid-covered services). The file is called the “MMA file” (after the Medicare Prescription Drug,
(
printed page 65747)
Improvement and Modernization Act of 2003) and is occasionally referred to as the “state phase-down file.” Federal regulations at
42 CFR 423.910
require states to submit files daily. The Medicare Advantage Prescription Drug (MAPD) State User Guide (SUG) contains technical guidance for the state and file layouts of the MMA request and response files. Regulations governing MMA file data collection require Medicaid agencies in each of the fifty states and the District of Columbia (hereafter referred to as states) to submit at least one monthly file, including all known dually eligible beneficiaries, and subsequent daily files that provide updates for changes in dual eligibility status (accretions, deletions, and changes).
This submission is a revision of the currently approved collection with technical revisions to the MAPD SUG.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106659; File No. SR-CBOE-2026-061]
(
printed page 65854)
October 13, 2026.
I. Introduction
On June 30, 2026, Cboe Exchange, Inc. (“Exchange” or “Cboe”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”), pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act” or “Exchange Act”)
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
a proposed rule change to allow the Exchange to list binary options overlying specified key performance indicators (“KPI(s)”) reported by certain issuers of stock (“binary KPI options”). The proposed rule change was published for comment in the
Federal Register
on July 15, 2026.
[
3
]
On August 26, 2024, pursuant to Section 19(b)(2) of the Act,
[
4
]
the Commission designated a longer period within which to approve the proposed rule change, disapprove the proposed rule change, or institute proceedings to determine whether to disapprove the proposed rule change.
[
5
]
The Commission received comments regarding the proposed rule change.
[
6
]
On October 1, 2026, the Exchange filed Amendment No. 1 to the proposed rule change, which replaces and supersedes the original filing in its entirety.
[
7
]
The Commission is publishing this notice and order to solicit comment on Amendment No. 1 in Sections II and III below, which sections are being published verbatim as filed by the Exchange, and to approve the proposed rule change, as modified by Amendment No. 1, on an accelerated basis.
[
8
]
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe Exchange, Inc. (the “Exchange” or “Cboe Options”) proposes to amend its Rules to permit the listing of binary options overlying key performance indicators (“KPIs”) reported by certain issuers of stock (“binary KPI options”). The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.
The text of the proposed rule change is also available on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
), the Exchange's website (
https://www.cboe.com/​us/​options/​regulation/​rule_​filings/​cone/​
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
III. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend its Rules to permit the listing of binary options overlying key performance indicators (“KPIs”) reported by certain issuers of stock (“binary KPI options”).
By way of background, binary options are based on the same framework as traditional, standardized options traded on the Exchange, except the payout of a binary option is a fixed amount contingent upon the occurrence of the option being in- or at-the-money rather than an amount based on the degree to which the option is in-the-money. As a result, payout at expiration of a binary option is an all-or-nothing occurrence.
Under current Exchange Rules, the Exchange may list binary options on broad-based indexes and the Cboe Magnificent 10 Index.
[
9
]
The Exchange proposes to amend its Rules to permit the listing of binary KPI options. Binary KPI options are European-style, cash-settled options contracts listed on an underlying KPI of an issuer. The exercise settlement value of a binary KPI option is determined not by the market price of the issuer's stock, but by whether a specific financial or operating metric that is reported by the issuer in an earnings-related filing submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) meets or exceeds a pre-specified strike level.
First, the Exchange proposes to adopt Chapter 4, Section I (Binary KPI Options) to describe binary KPI options. The Rules in proposed Chapter 4, Section I apply only to binary KPI options. All other Rules apply to the trading of binary KPI options, except as otherwise provided or the context otherwise requires.
The Exchange proposes to adopt Rule 4.80 (Definitions). Like other standardized options, binary KPI options have standardized terms that are established by the Exchange. Standardized terms for binary KPI options include the exercise criterion that is the condition or criterion of a binary KPI option, the exercise settlement amount (
i.e.,
payout amount), the strike price, the expiration date, the settlement type as A.M.-settlement or P.M.-settlement, the exercise style (as European-style), and the requirements used to determine if the KPI condition or criterion of a binary KPI option has been met (the “payout determination”
[
10
]
). The Exchange proposes to establish these terms in new Rule 4.80 and additional provisions related to binary KPI options in proposed Chapter 4, Section I, as described below.
The Exchange proposes to define a “binary KPI option” in new Rule 4.80 as a cash-settled option contract listed on an underlying KPI of an issuer with an exercise settlement amount that is
(
printed page 65855)
established at the creation of the option and with a settlement value that is determined by whether a specific KPI disclosed by the issuer in an earnings-related filing submitted to the Commission meets or exceeds its exercise price. Binary KPI options are paid out if the reported value of the applicable KPI (1) equals or is greater than (
i.e.,
the payout determination) the exercise price for a call binary KPI option or (2) is less than (
i.e.,
the payout determination) the exercise price for a put binary KPI option.
[
11
]
The Exchange also proposes to provide that unless the context dictates otherwise, the terms underlying security, equity, or index, or any variations of these terms, in the Rules mean issuer KPI for purposes of binary KPI options.
[
12
]
The Exchange proposes to define a “call binary KPI option” as an option contract that returns an exercise settlement amount if the settlement value of the underlying KPI is at or above the exercise price at expiration (
i.e.,
in- or at-the-money).
[
13
]
The Exchange proposes to define “exercise price” (also referred to as “strike price”) as the value
[
14
]
to which the settlement value of the underlying KPI is compared to determine whether the holder of a binary KPI option is entitled to the exercise settlement amount.
[
15
]
For binary KPI options, the exercise price is the exercise threshold of an option contract that establishes the number that is compared against the settlement value of the underlying KPI to determine if the cash payout amount (
i.e.,
the exercise settlement amount) will be paid out. In other words, binary KPI options will have a threshold number as the exercise price that will be used to determine if the exercise criterion of the binary KPI option has been met, in which case the option will be exercised and holders will receive the cash payout amount (
i.e.,
the exercise settlement amount). For binary KPI options, the exercise threshold will be a number that reflects or is compared to the underlying KPI of the binary option.
The Exchange proposes to define the term KPI (or “key performance indicator”) as a key financial or operating metric disclosed by an issuer in its earnings-related filings submitted to the Commission (
i.e.,
Form 8-K, Form 10-Q, or Form 10-K, as applicable).
The Exchange proposes to define “put binary KPI option” as an option contract that returns an exercise settlement amount if the settlement value of the underlying KPI is below the exercise price at expiration (
i.e.,
in-the-money).
[
16
]
The Exchange proposes to define “settlement value” as the value of the underlying KPI that is used to determine whether a binary KPI option is in-, at-, or out-of-the-money.
[
17
]
The proposed definition specifies that the “settlement value” is the value of the applicable KPI as disclosed in the applicable issuer's earnings-related filing submitted to the Commission on the applicable expiration date (for both A.M.-settled and P.M.-settled binary KPI options).
[
18
]
The Exchange designates the applicable KPI and the relevant reporting period (for example, a calendar quarter) at the time of listing a binary KPI option.
Proposed paragraph (b) of the settlement value definition provides if the applicable KPI is not reported or is otherwise unavailable on the expiration date,
[
19
]
settlement (including any payout of the exercise settlement amount) will occur in accordance with the Rules of the Clearing Corporation.
[
20
]
The alternative settlement procedures of the Clearing Corporation (as further discussed below) provide that if the KPI value needed to determine whether a binary KPI option is at- or in-the-money is not available, expiring contracts will be exercised but may result in delivery of an alternative exercise settlement amount. The alternative exercise settlement amount may be the last closing price of the binary KPI option (
i.e.,
the market valuation of the KPI event), meaning that the alternative exercise settlement amount will be between $0.01 and $1.00, rather than the expected $0.00 or $1.00. For example, if a KPI will not be reported by the KPI issuer, there is expiring open interest on binary KPI options on that KPI, and the last closing price of the binary KPI option was $0.76, the alternative settlement procedures of the Clearing Corporation provide that expiring binary KPI options may be exercised and settle at $0.76 rather than $1.00. If an option closing price is not available or is deemed by CCUS to be unreliable, the exercise criterion for binary option contracts on that KPI event will be deemed to have not been met, and the binary options will expire unexercised and worthless.
Additionally, proposed paragraph (c) of the settlement value definition states if an applicable KPI is restated after the expiration date and settlement of a binary KPI option, the settlement value (and the exercise settlement amount) of the binary KPI option does not change (as set forth in the Rules of the Clearing Corporation). In other words, the value of the applicable KPI as reported by the issuer on the applicable expiration date is final, and the amount paid (or not paid) at settlement will not change, regardless of whether the KPI is later restated by the issuer.
The Exchange proposes to add Rule 4.81 (Designation of Binary KPI Option Contracts) to identify the binary KPI options that may be listed for trading on the Exchange. Pursuant to proposed Rule 4.81(a), the Exchange may from time to time approve for listing and
(
printed page 65856)
trading on the Exchange any of the following binary KPI options contracts for the following issuers:
Company
KPI
                                 (each financial metric is measured in $ unless otherwise 
                                 specified)
Apple, Inc
Earnings per Share: Diluted; Total Net Sales; Net Sales by Category: iPhone; Net Sales by Category: Services; Net Sales by Reportable Segment: Americas; Net Sales by Reportable Segment: Greater China.

Robinhood Markets, Inc

SoFi Technologies, Inc
