Finally, the Exchange believes the proposed amendment to the hedge exemption provision is consistent with the Act because it facilitates legitimate hedging activity in binary KPI options. Because a liquidity provider simultaneously holding a short put and short call position in binary KPI options has taken opposing sides of the potential binary outcome (
i.e.,
the short call is at risk if the KPI is met, and the short put is at risk if the KPI is not met), the Exchange believes such a position represents a defined, bounded risk profile that does not present the same potential for manipulation or market disruption that position limits are designed to prevent. The Exchange believes it is reasonable to make the proposed hedge exemption available only to binary KPI positions held by Market-Makers. As described above, the current equity hedge exemption in Rule 8.30 is unavailable to Market-Makers for binary KPI options. The Exchange believes that offsetting binary KPI option creates a similar hedge to one to which the equity exemption is available. The Exchange believes the proposed hedge exemption (in addition to any other exemptions available under Rule 8.30) will allow Market-Makers to provide depth and liquidity in the marketplace for binary KPI options. The Exchange therefore believes the hedge exemption as proposed will encourage market-making activity and liquidity provision in binary KPI options while protecting investors and the public.
The Exchange also believes the proposed changes to Rule 8.43(f) are consistent with the Act. By establishing tailored reporting requirements for binary KPI options, the Exchange will be able to monitor TPH positions effectively and detect any accumulation of positions that may approach or exceed applicable limits to the benefit of investors. The Exchange believes it is consistent with just and equitable principles of trade for 100 binary KPI option contracts to equal one standard option contract for purposes of determining whether the report in Rule 8.43(a) is required given the relatively small size of binary KPI contracts compared to standard option contracts. As discussed above, proposed binary KPI options have a multiplier of one, while standard option contracts have a multiplier of 100. Therefore, the notional value of a binary KPI option is significantly less than the notional value of standard option contracts. For example, 200 contracts with a value of $1.00 with a multiplier of 100 would equate to $20,000 notional value, while 200 binary KPI option contracts with a value of $1.00 (which is the fixed maximum value of a binary KPI option contract) with a multiplier of one would equate to $200 notional value. Counting 100 binary KPI contracts as one standard option contract for purposes of this report effectively calibrates the reporting requirement so that investors are required to submit the report for an economically equivalent number of contracts, which promotes just and equitable principles of trade. The Exchange believes the proposal will provide the Exchange and regulators with visibility into large position concentrations in binary KPI options, preserving the ability to identify unusual activity and respond to any unforeseen concerns, while calibrating the threshold to a metric that is meaningful for this contract given its smaller multiplier relative to that of standard equity options. The Exchange believes this reporting framework, coupled with the proposed position limits amendments, provides a fully adequate regulatory framework for these instruments.
Further, as noted above, the Exchange believes it has an adequate surveillance program in place to surveil for any potentially heightened insider trading or manipulation risks that may be presented by the proposed binary KPI options. The Exchange notes that the settlement value of a binary KPI option is sourced from the issuer's earnings-related filing submitted to the Commission. The values of these KPIs are produced through the accounting and reporting processes of the issuer, subject to independent audit prior to submission to the Commission. Because settlement is decoupled from the market price of the underlying security, no amount of trading activity in that security could alter the revenue, earnings, or other metric that determines whether the exercise criterion of a binary KPI option is satisfied. Any manipulation of the reported KPI would constitute securities fraud and expose the issuer to liability under federal securities law, separate and apart from any exchange-related violation.
Moreover, the specifically proposed binary KPI options present a more defined surveillance profile than other event contracts available in the market today. Because settlement is tied to a well-defined set of issuer-KPI metrics contained in earnings-related filings submitted to the Commission, the relevant surveillance framework operates as a focused subset of the insider trading surveillances the Exchange already applies to standard equity options. The legal prohibition on trading in the issuer's securities, including options, while in possession of MNPI about an unreported KPI is not novel, but rather the same prohibition the Exchange enforces today for standard equity options overlying the issuer's stock.
The Exchange believes the proposed binary KPI options will serve as a vehicle to hedge idiosyncratic, event-
(
printed page 65875)
specific risk embedded in the specific issuer KPIs. Standard equity options are calibrated to the price of the underlying security and capture a full spectrum of factors or risks which may affect the issuer's value, such as macroeconomic conditions or sector dynamics. Because equity option pricing incorporates this full spectrum, a participant seeking to hedge exposure to a single, discrete KPI outcome cannot do so using standard equity options as precisely as the participant could with binary KPI options. Settlement of a binary KPI option is determined solely by whether a specified-issuer KPI meets a defined threshold, so the contract effectively isolates certain individual risks an investor may seek to manage. For example, consider an investor holding a long-term position in a particular issuer stock, who believes the issuer's quarterly revenue will fall short of expectations (for reasons unrelated to the issuer's long-term prospects). The investor may utilize the binary KPI option to hedge more precisely against the near-term risk without disruption to the underlying equity position. This targeted hedging utility represents a distinct and additive function relative to existing listed products, which the Exchange believes will serve the interests of investors and provide an efficient mechanism for managing event-specific, KPI-driven risk.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change will facilitate transactions in securities, remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, protect investors and the public interest, because it will provide investors with a securities exchange-listed investment choice for these instruments, offering price transparency and the regulatory protections of a national securities exchange. The Exchange believes the proposed rule change will permit investors to manage their risk exposures and carry out their investment objectives on a securities exchange with more flexibility and broader applicability. The Exchange also believes the proposed rule change will promote competition, as it will meet demands of investors that currently may trade products structured in substantively the same manner as the proposed binary KPI options in other markets (as further discussed below). Binary KPI options would provide investors with a straightforward means of expressing a directional view on key financial and operating metrics. The Exchange further believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest, as binary KPI options would be subject to the Exchange's existing rules governing the listing and trading of options. The Exchange believes expanding the universe of binary options will benefit investors, particularly retail investors and other investors who prefer simplicity, as a complementary offering to current exchange-traded options.
The proposed rule change will permit the Exchange to list binary KPI options on a national securities exchange as alternatives to products that are structured in substantially the same manner as binary options currently available in the OTC market and on other platforms. The Exchange understands investors have traded binary options similar to the proposed binary options in OTC markets for many years but may prefer to trade such options in a listed environment to receive the benefits of trading listing options. These benefits include: (1) enhanced efficiency in initiating and closing out positions; (2) increased market transparency; and (3) heightened contra-party creditworthiness. The Exchange believes the proposed rule change may encourage liquidity to shift from the OTC market onto the Exchange, which the Exchange believes would increase market transparency as well as enhance the process of price discovery conducted on the Exchange through increased order flow. The proposed rule change is intended to provide a market for binary KPI options as a standardized product without the credit risk of an individual issuer. By providing a listed and standardized market for more classes of binary options, the Exchange seeks to attract investors who desire the simplicity of a binary option with the certainty and safeguards of a regulated and standardized marketplace. Additionally, unlike an OTC binary option, contra-party credit risk for Exchange-listed binary KPI options is significantly reduced through the issuance and guarantee of the contracts by a registered clearing agency. Further, as an exchange-traded option, binary options will have the advantage of liquidity provided by Market-Makers, which the Exchange believes may lead to tighter spreads than those in the OTC market. The Exchange also believes that standardization will enable more interested parties to become market participants.
In addition to the OTC market, various market platforms that are not registered as national securities exchanges currently offer products structured in substantively the same manner as binary options that the Exchange may list pursuant to current Rules and as proposed. These platforms offer binary option products overlying issuer KPIs, which may be settled at varying points of the day (not just at the open and close of the trading day). However, as these venues are not national securities exchanges, they do not offer investors the benefits of centralized liquidity, market transparency, or securities regulations intended to protect investors. The Exchange believes listing competitive products on a national securities exchange would create a centralized and standardized marketplace for these products, which promotes price discovery and transparency, within an established and appropriate regulatory framework designed to afford investors in securities with important protections. In other words, the Exchange believes its proposal offers a more transparent platform than the OTC market or other market platforms offer. It would contribute to leveling the playing field with these alternative markets and provide investors with safeguards associated with Commission and SRO oversight of the trading activity in the proposed exchange-listed binary KPI options.
Ultimately, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change will provide investors with greater trading tools and opportunities and flexibility, resulting in investors having additional means to carry out their investment objectives and manage their risk exposures through products listed and traded on a national securities exchange. The Exchange believes the proposed rule change will offer market participants a simplified, transparent, and limited risk investment choice that may be more aligned with their specific timing needs, investment and hedging strategies, and risk tolerances. The Exchange believes it benefits the investing public to continue to enhance its listed product offerings to respond to continuously changing needs of investors and to a continuously changing competitive environment.
A robust and competitive market requires exchanges to respond to investors' evolving needs by regularly improving their offerings. When Congress charged the Commission with supervising the development of a “national market system” for securities, Congress stated its intent that the “national market system evolve through the interplay of competitive forces as unnecessary regulatory restrictions are
(
printed page 65876)
removed.”
[
116
]
Consistent with this purpose, Congress and the Commission have repeatedly stated their preference for competition, rather than regulatory intervention to determine products and services in the securities markets.
[
117
]
This consistent and considered judgment of Congress and the Commission is correct, particularly in light of evidence of robust competition in the options trading industry. The fact that an exchange proposed something new is a reason to be receptive, not skeptical—innovation is the lifeblood of a vibrant competitive market—and that is particularly so given the continued internationalization of the securities markets, as exchanges and other platforms continue to implement new products and services to compete not only in the United States but throughout the world. Options exchanges continuously adopt new and different products and trading services in response to industry demands to attract order flow and to increase their trading volume. This competition has led to a growth in investment choices, which ultimately benefits the marketplace and the public. The Exchange believes the proposed rule change will help further competition by providing market participants with yet another investment option for options listed on a national securities exchange.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on intramarket competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act, because binary KPI options will be available to all market participants who wish to trade such options on the same terms and in the same manner (including with respect to the payout terms and amount). All market participants will be subject to the same rules applicable to binary KPI options, as described in this proposed rule change. Except as set forth in the proposed rule change, binary KPI options will trade in the same manner as other options, including binary index options, on the Exchange.
The Exchange does not believe the proposed rule change will impose any burden on intermarket competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act, because other options exchanges may propose similar products. Additionally, as noted above, substantively similar products to the proposed binary KPI options are available in the OTC market and various other markets.
The Exchange notes that it operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily direct order flow to competing venues who offer similar products. The Exchange believes the proposed rule change will provide investors with a comparable alternative to the OTC market and other venues. The Exchange believes it may be a more attractive alternative to the OTC market and these other venues, as market participants will benefit from being able to trade these options in a securities exchange environment, which provides, among other things: (1) enhanced efficiency in initiating and closing out positions; (2) increased market transparency; (3) heightened contra-party creditworthiness; and (4) investor protections of the securities regulatory framework. As a result, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change may relieve any burden on, or otherwise promote, competition, as it will allow the Exchange to offer a securities exchange-listed alternative to the products currently available in these other markets.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received written comments on the proposed rule change.

Proposed Exchange Rule
(

4.81 sets forth the classes of binary KPI options that the Exchange could list by delineating each issuer by name and, for each issuer, each KPI of that issuer upon which the Exchange would be permitted to list binary options. Options overlying a given issuer KPI listed in proposed Exchange Rule 4.81(a) would represent a class of options that is separate from other classes of options overlying the stock of the issuer or other KPIs of the issuer listed in proposed Exchange Rule 4.81(a).

Option contracts overlying particular issuer KPIs would permit more granular and varied exposure to issuer performance as reflected in the issuer's stock price than that provided by option contracts overlying the issuer's stock. The proposed binary KPI options could enable more flexible and bespoke management of positions by allowing market participants to gain exposure to, or hedge against, specific aspects of an issuer's performance. For example, the proposed binary KPI options could allow a long-term investor in the stock of an issuer to hedge against the short-term risk that the issuer's stock price might decline due to one of the KPIs in proposed Exchange Rule 4.81, such as reduced revenue or net sales for a given quarter. D. Position Limits and Other Safeguards
Position limits serve as a regulatory tool designed to deter manipulative schemes and mitigate the risk of adverse market impact surrounding the use of options. Since the inception of standardized options trading, the options exchanges have had rules limiting the aggregate number of options contracts that a member or customer may hold or exercise.
[
175
]
Proposed Exchange Rule 8.36 would provide that, in determining compliance with Exchange Rule 8.30, the position limit for binary KPI options is 25,000 standard option contracts, and 100 binary KPI options contracts equal one standard option contract.
[
176
]
Proposed Exchange Rule 8.36 also would provide that, for position limit purposes, a given binary KPI option position would not be aggregated with: (i) a position with a different expiration date for the same binary KPI option for the same issuer;
[
177
]
(ii) a position in a different binary KPI option for the same issuer;
[
178
]
or (iii) a position in a non-binary option overlying the stock of the issuer.
[
179
]
The Exchange's proposed position limits and related safeguards for binary KPI options reflect a reasonable approach to address the potential for manipulation of binary KPI options, which have not been previously listed on the Exchange, and are therefore reasonably designed to protect investors and the public interest. And this approach is consistent with longstanding listed options market requirements for equity option position limits. The Commission approved the Exchange's current equity option position limits, set forth in Exchange Rule 8.30, in 2005, and these position limits subsequently were replicated by other options exchanges.
[
180
]
A position limit of 25,000 contracts is the most conservative limit currently set forth in Exchange Rule 8.30 (and the identical rules of other exchanges).
[
181
]
Because of the difference in contract multipliers—equity options have a contract multiplier of 100 and the proposed binary KPI options have a contract multiplier of one—counting 100 binary KPI contracts as one standard option contract for purposes of position limits would calibrate position limits appropriately so that investors may hold positions in binary KPI options of an issuer that are proportional to the number of contracts they may hold in options on the stock of that issuer. Moreover, current Exchange rules do not require aggregation of equity option positions across different classes for position limit purposes, just as proposed Exchange Rule 8.36 would not require aggregation across different binary KPI option classes.

182
]
Further,
(
printed page 65881)
pursuant to the rules of other exchanges, a 25,000-contract position limit applies to binary equity options without aggregation with other options positions overlying the same or similar security.

183
]

185

The Exchange's proposed approach to position limits for binary KPI options appropriately accounts for the fact that binary KPI options have not previously been listed on the Exchange. Accordingly, the Commission finds that these mechanisms will sufficiently protect investors and prevent fraud and manipulation, and, in particular, help to deter insider trading, consistent with Sections 6(b)(1) and 6(b)(5) of the Act.

and (v) in accordance with the Linkage Plan and Exchange Rules 5.65 through 5.67, the Exchange's system is designed, at all times, to prevent trade-throughs and avoid displaying locked/crossed markets, and in the event that binary KPI options become multi-listed options, Users may designate an order for routing (or not) pursuant to Exchange Rule 5.36.

F. Product Classification
Section 3(a)(10) of the Exchange Act defines “security” to include, in part, “any put, call, straddle, option, or privilege on any security, certificate of deposit, or group or index of securities (including any interest therein or based on the value thereof).”
[
215
]
The proposed binary options overlying specific KPIs reported by specific issuers of stock, as the Exchange proposes to structure, list, and trade them, may be categorized as (i) options on a (ii) security, consistent with the definition of “security” in Section 3(a)(10) of the Exchange Act.
[
216
]
This Commission finding speaks solely to the listing and trading of these specific binary option contracts on a securities exchange that lists and trades standardized options on securities in compliance with the securities laws.
First, the specific binary KPI options proposed by the Exchange may be categorized as options. In the absence of a definition of the term “option” in the Exchange Act or Commission rules, the Commission's analysis as to whether an exchange-proposed product is an option previously has focused on whether the facts and circumstances related to the product reflect the presence of typical characteristics of options.
[
217
]
Such characteristics are present here. As described above, the proposed binary KPI options would be listed and traded on the Exchange pursuant to rules that set forth the type of standardized terms typically applied to exchange-listed security options and that apply to security options already listed and traded on the Exchange. These terms include a traditional option call and put contract structure, each of which may be bought or sold, as well as standardized terms for exercise prices, expirations, series listing, and settlement. Through these standardized terms, the proposed binary KPI options present as option contracts, including that the buyer of a binary KPI option contract pays to the seller a nonrefundable premium, has rights but no further obligations under the contract, and has no further risk exposure. Furthermore, the trading of binary KPI options as standardized options on the Exchange, if implemented, would occur subject to broader regulatory features typical of standardized securities option trading. One such feature would be centralized clearing of binary KPI option transactions by a securities options clearing agency that is registered with the Commission pursuant to the Exchange Act. Another such feature would be an options disclosure document, prepared pursuant to Rule 9b-1 under the Exchange Act, which would disclose the risks and characteristics of the proposed binary KPI options, and which broker-dealers would be required to provide to any given customer before accepting an order from the customer to purchase or sell a binary KPI option contract.
[
218
]
Second, the specific binary KPI options as proposed by the Exchange may be categorized as options on a security.
[
219
]
The binary KPI options included in the Amended Proposal are limited to issuers with a class of equity securities that are listed for trading on a national securities exchange. The option prong of the “security” definition includes any option on a security (including any interest therein or based on the value thereof).
[
220
]
As the Commission has stated before, the Commission interprets “based on the value [of a security or securities]” in the option prong of Section 3(a)(10) of the Exchange Act “to include any option whose pricing in the secondary market moves in relation to the value of the underlying security or securities of the option in question.”
[
221
]
In this case, each proposed binary KPI option is based on the issuer's disclosure of the KPI in the issuer's earnings-related reports filed with or furnished to the Commission (including KPIs such as earnings, sales, revenue, operating margin, net income, interest income, credit losses, trading volume, and free
(
printed page 65884)
cash flow).
[
222
]
It is well-established that the value of an issuer's stock moves in relation to issuer performance disclosures like those underlying the proposed binary KPI options.
[
223
]
Accordingly, in this case, each Cboe-proposed binary KPI option is correlated with the value of the issuer's stock,
[
224
]
and it is expected that the price of each Cboe-proposed binary KPI option will move in relation to the value of the issuer's stock during the life of the option contract.
[
225
]
One commenter states that, unlike the standardized binary options that currently trade, the proposed binary KPI options do not “settle” on the price or value of a security.
[
226
]
The commenter suggests that because the Commission and the CFTC have issued a joint request for comment related to the further definition of “swap” and “security-based swap”
[
227
]
the Commission should not approve the Amended Proposal at this time.
[
228
]
This order does not address what may be similar products with the same underlying KPIs as the binary options described in the order structured in different ways.
[
229
]
The determination of when a product falls within Exchange Act Section 3(a)(10) (including whether it is based on a security, including any interest therein and based on the value thereof) is within the Commission's statutory authority. As detailed above, the proposed product meets the definition of an option on a security, and the Commission finds that the Amended Proposal is consistent with the Act. As such, as directed by the statute, the Commission must approve the Exchange's rule filing.
[
230
]
The Exchange's proposed binary KPI options may be listed as options on a security also because they are options on an interest in, or based on the value of an interest in, a security or securities within the meaning of Section 3(a)(10) of the Exchange Act. As the Commission has previously stated, “the concept of an `interest in' a security plainly includes rights generating a pecuniary interest in a security, such as the right to a dividend payment or bond (coupon) payment.”
[
231
]
Further, “merely because the option does not transfer ownership of the interest or right in a security—but instead becomes in-the-money and provides a cash payment if certain security rights are triggered—does not mean the option is not on an interest in a security.”
[
232
]
Each proposed binary KPI option provides a cash payout based on the disclosed KPI, and because the KPI is tied to a pecuniary interest in the issuer's stock, the binary KPI option is an option on an interest in, or based on the value of an interest in, that stock. For example, stockholders have a pro rata claim to a residual interest in the net assets of the issuer, which is an interest in the security.
[
233
]
The value of that interest is tied to measures such as earnings per share, which is a profitability measure
[
234
]
and may be considered by investors, together with other financial and operating information.
[
235
]
The Commission is cognizant that similar products with the same underlying KPIs as the binary options described in this order may be structured in different ways and be subject to CFTC jurisdiction. As emphasized above, the Commission's findings in this order address solely the listing and trading of Cboe's specific binary option contracts on a securities exchange that lists and trades standardized options on securities in compliance with the securities laws. The Commission's findings in this order are non-exclusive and do not address any context beyond the proposed rule change pending before the Commission. As noted above, the Commission's order does not foreclose other markets from structuring derivative instruments overlying KPIs as other products.
In that regard, for the reasons discussed above, the Exchange's proposed binary KPI options may be
(
printed page 65885)
listed as securities options within the meaning of the definition of “security” in Section 3(a)(10) of the Exchange Act. As a result, the Exchange's proposal to list and trade binary KPI options as securities options is consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act in that it is not designed to regulate by virtue of any authority conferred by the Exchange Act matters not related to the purposes of the Exchange Act or the administration of the exchange.

VII. Designation of the Proposed Binary KPI Options Pursuant to Rule 9b-1
Rule 9b-1 establishes a disclosure framework for standardized options that are traded on a national securities exchange and cleared through a registered clearing agency. Under this framework, the exchange on which a standardized option is listed and traded must prepare an ODD that, among other things, identifies the issuer and describes the uses, mechanics, and risks of options trading, in language that can be easily understood by the general investing public. The ODD is treated as a substitute for the traditional prospectus. A broker-dealer must provide a copy of the ODD to each customer at the time of, or before, approval of the customer's account for trading any standardized option.
[
239
]
Any amendment to the ODD must be distributed to each customer whose account is approved for trading the options class for which the ODD relates.
[
240
]
Under Rule 9b-1, use of the ODD is limited to “standardized options” for which there is an effective registration statement on Form S-20 under the Securities Act or that are exempt from registration.
[
241
]
Rule 9b-1 defines “standardized options” as “options contracts trading on a national securities exchange . . . which relate to options classes the terms of which are limited to specific expiration dates and exercise prices, or such other securities as the Commission may, by order, designate.” The Commission specifically reserved in Rule 9b-1 the ability to designate as standardized options other securities “that the Commission believes should be included within the options disclosure framework.”
[
242
]
The proposed binary KPI options meet the Rule 9b-1 definition of standardized options because they would be traded on a national securities exchange and limited to specific expiration dates and exercise prices.
[
243
]
More broadly, the proposed binary KPI options would be listed and traded on the Exchange with key standardized terms that characterize standardized options, including, aside from specific expiration dates and exercise prices, terms relating to the issuance of puts and calls, minimum strike intervals, initial and additional series listings,
(
printed page 65886)
contract adjustments, time of issuance, and settlement. Further, the fact that the proposed binary KPI options would be centrally cleared supports their treatment as standardized options.
For the avoidance of doubt, however, the Commission also hereby designates the Exchange's proposed binary KPI options as standardized options for purposes of Rule 9b-1 under the Act.
[
244
]

The assessment of whether a financial instrument is a security-based swap or a linked security depends, in part, on the exclusions from the definition of “swap.” There are several exclusions from the definition of “swap” relating to securities. To the extent a financial instrument falls into one of these exclusions, it is not a swap and, therefore, is not a security-based swap. Information that moves the value of an issuer's stock will move the value of options on the issuer's stock because the value of a stock option is based largely on the value of the underlying stock. The proposed KPIs measure the performance of the issuer and help to determine the value of the issuer's stock. Accordingly, the value of the proposed KPI options will be correlated with each other and with the value of the issuer's stock. At the same time, as discussed above (

supra
), a given binary KPI option position would not be aggregated with a position in an option overlying the stock of issuer. This would not enable market participants to utilize binary KPI options to circumvent existing position limits for options on the stock of an issuer because binary KPI options and options on the stock of an issuer are options on different underliers that provide related, but different, exposures. Purchasing options on one or more KPIs of an issuer would not provide a market participant with a means to acquire additional stock of the issuer, nor would the exercise of such options affect the price of the issuer's stock. Rather, the proposed KPI options will provide exposure to, or a hedge against, specific aspects of an issuer's performance.

National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS)
Title:
Agricultural Surveys Program—Substantive Change.
OMB Control Number:
0535-0213.
Summary of Collection:
General authority for these data collection activities is granted under U.S. Code Title 7, Section 2204 which specifies that “The Secretary of Agriculture shall procure and preserve all information concerning agriculture which he can obtain . . . by the collection of statistics . . .”. The primary objective of the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) is to provide data users with timely and reliable agricultural production and economic statistics, as well as environmental and specialty agricultural related statistics. To accomplish this objective, NASS relies on the use of diverse surveys that show changes within the farming industry over time.
NASS is requesting a substantive change to the 2027 June Area Survey and Agricultural Coverage Evaluation Survey (ACES) data-collection instruments. ACES is conducted only during the Census of Agriculture reference year, which occurs every five years. Because the June Area Survey and ACES collect substantially overlapping information, NASS plans to use a modified ACES questionnaire for both surveys in 2027.
The modified questionnaire will retain selected June Area Survey questions to ensure that all required data items are collected. Using a common questionnaire for both data collections will improve census coverage, increase operational efficiency, and reduce respondent burden by coordinating related data-collection activities.
NASS is requesting revisions to the race and ethnicity questions for both the June Area Survey and ACES. In light of OMB's March 27, 2026 announcement of a one-year extension to submit an Action Plan for compliance with the updates to Statistical Policy Directive
(
printed page 65716)
No. 15,
Standards for Maintaining, Collecting, and Presenting Federal Data on Race and Ethnicity,
NASS will use the 1997 standards in Agricultural Surveys Program and will use the delayed deadline to continue developing implementation plans for the 2024 standards. Updating the race and ethnicity questions consistently across both questionnaires will support efficient data collection, reduce potential respondent confusion, and maintain consistency for census coverage purposes.
Need and Use of the Information:
The surveys provide the basis for estimates of the current season's crop and livestock production and supplies of grain in storage. Crop and livestock statistics help develop a stable economic atmosphere and reduce risk for production, marketing, and distribution operations. These commodities affect the well-being of the nation's farmers, commodities markets, and national and global agricultural policy. Users of agricultural statistics are farm organizations, agribusiness, state and national farm policy makers, and foreign buyers of agricultural products but the primary user of the statistical information is the producer. Agricultural statistics are also used to plan and administer other related federal and state programs in such areas as school lunch program, conservation, foreign trade, education, and recreation. Collecting the information less frequent would eliminate needed data to keep the government and agricultural industry abreast of changes at the state and national levels.

Farms and Ranches.
Number of Respondents:
596,600.
Frequency of Responses:
Reporting: Quarterly; Semi-annually; Monthly; Annually.
Total Burden Hours:
207,289.

Summary of Collection:
The primary functions of the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) are to prepare and issue State and national estimates of crop and livestock production, disposition, and prices and to collect information on related environmental and economic factors. Information from federally and non- federally inspected slaughter plants are used to estimate total red meat production. NASS will use a Federally and non-Federally inspected livestock slaughter survey to collect data.

plants are combined to estimate total red meat production, consisting of the number of head slaughtered and live weights of cattle, calves, hogs, sheep/lambs, goats, and buffalo/bison. SUMMARY:
This document announces that the Coast Guard will not require the electronic submission requirement for mariner course completion data until at least November 25, 2028, because the system for providing the electronic submission is not yet fully operational. The Coast Guard will notify the public through the
Federal Register
before requiring the electronic submission of course completion data.
DATES:
The requirement in
46 CFR 10.403(a)(7)
to electronically submit mariner course completion data will not be implemented before November 25, 2028.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For information about this document, call or email Mr. Brian T. Eichelberger, Office of Merchant Mariner Credentialing, Coast Guard; telephone 571-608-2071, email
Brian.T.Eichelberger@uscg.mil
.
Background and Discussion
The Coast Guard issues Merchant Mariner Credentials to mariners who have met the regulatory requirements for individual endorsement(s), as described in
46 CFR parts 10
,
11
,
12
, and
13
. The general standards for Coast Guard-approved courses and programs are found in
46 CFR 10.403
. On November 25, 2024, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Coast Guard, issued a final rule titled “Electronic Submission of Mariner Course Completion Data”
[
1
]
hereafter, “2024 final rule.”
The 2024 final rule amended
46 CFR 10.403
to require Coast Guard-approved training providers to electronically submit the mariner course completion data listed in
46 CFR 10.403(b)(7)(i)
through
(v)
to the National Maritime Center within 5 business days after a student completes a Coast Guard-approved course or program. The 2024 final rule stated Coast Guard-approved training providers were required to comply with this regulation by November 25, 2026.
At the time the 2024 final rule was published, the Coast Guard anticipated using the Homeport online portal as the mechanism for the electronic submission of course completion data, pending development of an updated information technology system. However, on April 12, 2025, the Coast Guard decommissioned the Homeport online portal because of increased operating costs, system obsolescence, and cybersecurity concerns.
On September 14, 2026, the Coast Guard announced the initial release of Navita
TM
, a new digital platform designed to streamline the application and issuance of merchant mariner credentials.
[
2
]
Navita
TM
is intended to replace the current labor-intensive manual mariner credentialing process.
Navita
TM
will include a dedicated mariner training provider module that will facilitate electronic submission of mariner course completion data as required by
46 CFR 10.403(b)(7)
. The Coast Guard expects the Navita
TM
mariner training provider module to become fully operational in January 2028. Accordingly, the Coast Guard expects to begin the requirement for electronic submission of mariner course completion data on November 25, 2028.
Before requiring the electronic submission of course completion data, the Coast Guard will notify the public through publication in the
Federal Register
announcing the availability of the Navita
TM
mariner training provider capability and will provide guidance to facilitate meeting the requirements for electronic submission. In the interim, mariners should continue to submit their course completion certificates to the National Maritime Center with their merchant mariner credential applications.
This notice is issued under authority of
5 U.S.C. 552(a)
.
R.C. Compher,

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it establishes Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Ranch at Double Gates Airport, Coleman, TX, to support IFR operations.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-9213 in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 51403
; August 10, 2026) proposing to establish Class E airspace at Ranch at Double Gates Airport, Coleman, TX. Interested parties were invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. No comments were received.
Incorporation by Reference
Class E airspace designations are published in paragraph 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in
14 CFR 71.1
on an annual basis. This document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These amendments will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO
(
printed page 65681)

ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Rule
This action modifies
14 CFR part 71
by establishing Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface within a 7.2-mile radius of Ranch at Double Gates Airport, Coleman, TX. This action is the result of instrument procedures being developed for this heliport to support IFR operations.
Regulatory Notices and Analyses
The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. It, therefore: (1) is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
; (2) is not a “significant rule” under DOT Order 2100.6B, “Rulemaking and Guidance Procedure” (March 10, 2025); and (3) is expected to result in, at most, de minimis costs from compliance with applicable operating requirements or minor flight rerouting for operators choosing to navigate around the controlled airspace. Since these amendments are routine and the expected impact to operators is de minimis, the FAA certifies that this rule, when promulgated, does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
Environmental Review
The FAA has determined that this action qualifies for categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, “FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures,” paragraph B-2.5(a), which categorically excludes from further environmental impact review rulemaking actions that designate or modify classes of airspace areas, airways, routes, and reporting points (see
14 CFR part 71
, Designation of Class A, B, C, D, and E Airspace Areas; Air Traffic Service Routes; and Reporting Points); and paragraph B-2.5(k), which categorically excludes from further environmental impact review the publication of existing air traffic control procedures that do not essentially change existing tracks, create new tracks, change altitude, or change concentration of aircraft on these tracks. Additionally, the FAA determined that this action is not expected to result in any potentially significant environmental impacts, and no extraordinary circumstances exist that warrant preparation of an environmental assessment.

Scope.

It may additionally be termed Accelerator CZ, CBTS, Thiohexam, HIP4, Curax, DURAX, Conaca, Conach, Conacs, or Celacs. A CBS assay or sample most commonly reflects a concentration of 94 to 99 percent. CBS is most commonly in the form of an off-white or light gray powder, oiled powder, or granule, though CBS imported in a different color or form is included in the scope. CBS typically has a melting point of 90 to 110 °C and a molecular weight of 264.4 g/mol. CBS may be imported in a solution of benzene, ethanol, or acetone. CBS has the chemical formula C

AGENCY:
Food and Drug Administration, HHS.
ACTION:
Notice of public meeting; request for information and comments.
SUMMARY:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA, the Agency, or we) is announcing a public meeting entitled “Fit-for-Purpose Rare Disease Framework Initiative”. Convened by the Reagan-Udall Foundation for, and in collaboration with FDA, the meeting will focus on developing a fit-for-purpose framework for the development and regulatory review of rare disease therapies. There will be an opportunity to request to provide public comments at the meeting. In addition, FDA is establishing a public docket to collect feedback on and input related to its Rare Disease Framework Initiative.
DATES:
The hybrid public meeting will be held on October 28, 2026, from 1 to 5 p.m. Eastern Time, and will take place in-person and virtually. Either electronic or written comments must be submitted by December 11, 2026. See the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section for registration information.
ADDRESSES:
The hybrid public meeting will be held in-person at the FDA White Oak Campus, 10903 New Hampshire Ave., White Oak Conference Center, Bldg. 2, Rm. 2047, Silver Spring, MD 20993-0002, and virtually using the Zoom platform. Entrance for the public meeting participants (non-FDA employees) is through Building 1 where routine security check procedures will be performed. For security and parking information, please refer to
https://www.fda.gov/​about-fda/​visitor-information
and
https://www.fda.gov/​about-fda/​visitor-information/​visitor-parking-and-campus-map
.
You may submit comments as follows. Please note that late, untimely filed comments will not be considered. The
https://www.regulations.gov
electronic filing system will accept comments until 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time at the end of December 11, 2026. Comments received by mail/hand delivery/courier (for written/paper submissions) will be considered timely if they are received on or before that date.

.

https://www.regulations.gov
will be posted to the docket unchanged. Because your comment will be made public, you are solely responsible for ensuring that your comment does not include any confidential information that you or a third party may not wish to be posted, such as medical information, your or anyone else's Social Security number, or confidential business information, such as a manufacturing process. Please note that if you include your name, contact information, or other information that identifies you in the body of your comments, that information will be posted on

.
If you want to submit a comment with confidential information that you do not wish to be made available to the public, submit the comment as a written/paper submission and in the manner detailed (see “Written/Paper Submissions” and “Instructions”).
(

Dockets Management Staff (HFA-305), Food and Drug Administration, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
FDA is announcing the launch of its Rare Disease Framework Initiative (Framework Initiative) to develop a regulatory framework purpose-built for rare disease therapies. Roughly 1 in 10 Americans lives with a rare disease, and only approximately 5 percent of rare conditions have an FDA-approved treatment. Developing therapies for rare diseases can present scientific and practical challenges, including small patient populations, limited understanding of certain diseases, and disease heterogeneity. FDA's Framework Initiative will respond to these challenges via a holistic approach that approaches regulatory review according to the particularities of each product based on specific disease state, product type, patient population, and attainable evidence.
The Framework Initiative—spearheaded by the Rare Disease Innovation Hub, the Office of the Commissioner, the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER), and the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER)—will result in a rare disease drug development and review process that:
1. Provides greater clarity, consistency, and predictability for drug developers, patients, disease advocates, and researchers regarding rare disease regulatory decision-making
through tailored guidance and transparent communication based on the latest science.
2. Embeds the patient voice both early and at clearly defined milestones in the development and review process for rare disease therapies
such that both sponsors and reviewers can benefit from patient perspectives on disease burden, benefit-risk priorities, and meaningful measures of progress.
3. Further leverages external expertise to support a tailored approach in regulatory review,
especially for rare conditions with very small patient populations and limited understanding of natural history, as a structural feature to direct FDA reviewers in customizing their decision-making to each specific development program, product, and disease state.
4. Builds shared resources, robust training, and institutional knowledge on rare disease drug development and review
to ensure consistency in drug development and review.
5. Applies risk-based approaches, particularly to chemistry, manufacturing, and controls review and pre-approval inspections,
to support earlier patient access without compromising rigorous quality, safety, and effectiveness standards.
6. Champions the use of cutting-edge science, novel methods and clinical trial designs, and innovative statistical approaches in the development of rare disease therapies
via guidance, transparent communication, and programming that reflects FDA's commitment to partnering with rare disease innovators to accelerate patient access to rare disease therapies.
II. Issues for Consideration and Request for Information
FDA is seeking feedback from the public—including rare disease drug developers, patients living with rare diseases and their caregivers, disease advocates, and researchers—on persistent challenges for the development of rare disease therapies, as well as input on how a tailored approach to regulatory review might mitigate these challenges. Feedback will inform development of the framework and potential implementation actions, which may include new or revised guidance documents related to rare disease drug development and regulatory review, revisions to FDA's regulations, training for FDA review staff, and organizational enhancements.
This Request for Information and Comments is being published in conjunction with a public meeting on October 28, 2026, to solicit feedback on the Rare Disease Framework Initiative. Interested parties may provide feedback on FDA's Rare Disease Framework Initiative by requesting to provide public comments at the public meeting, providing comments in the public docket that will be open from October 28 through December 11, 2026, or both. Registration information for the October 28, 2026, free public meeting, including information about how to request to provide public comments, can be found at the following web address:
https://www.fda.gov/​news-events/​fda-meetings-conferences-and-workshops/​fda-rare-disease-framework-initiative-public-meeting-10282026
.
In-person attendance is based on space availability, with priority given to early registrants. Early
(
printed page 65752)
registration is recommended because seating is limited; therefore, FDA may limit the number of participants from each organization. Registrants will receive confirmation when they have been accepted. If you need special accommodations due to a disability, please email
rdinnovationhub@fda.hhs.gov
no later than October 26, 2026, 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time.
FDA welcomes suggestions, ideas, and comments regarding CDER and CBER's roles in rare disease drug development and review. Below are four broad focus areas outlined in the Framework Initiative. We seek suggestions and comments within these topic areas and ask that you be as specific as possible in your feedback or recommendation. To help FDA review comments efficiently, please identify the topic area to which you are responding by its associated number. If you are responding to more than one topic area, please identify each topic area to which you are responding:
1. Fit-for-purpose review of rare disease therapies based on attainable evidence, particular disease state, and population.
2. Consistency and predictability of FDA's rare disease drug development and review regulatory requirements.
3. FDA engagements with external parties—including patients, disease experts, and researchers—to inform review decision-making for rare disease therapies.
4. Considerations for chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC) specific to rare disease therapies.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) determines that high purity dissolving pulp from Norway is being, or is likely to be, sold in the United States at less than fair value (LTFV). The period of investigation is July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025.
DATES:
Applicable October 16, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Braeden Lowe, AD/CVD Operations, Office V, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-9124.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On May 27, 2026, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
its preliminary affirmative determination in the LTFV investigation of high purity dissolving pulp from Norway and postponed the final determination until 135 days after the date of publication of the
Preliminary Determination.
[
1
]
Accordingly, the deadline for this final determination is now October 9, 2026. We invited interested parties to comment on the
Preliminary Determination.
[
2

Preliminary Determination,
as well as a full discussion of the issue raised by parties for this final determination, may be found in the Issues and Decision Memorandum.
[
3

The Issues and Decision Memorandum is a public document and is made available to the public via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty
(
printed page 65728)

.
In addition, a complete version of the Issues and Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at

Scope of the Investigation
The product covered by this investigation is high purity dissolving pulp from Norway. For a complete description of the scope of this investigation,
see
Appendix I.
Scope Comments
During the course of this investigation, Commerce received scope comments from parties. Commerce issued a Preliminary Scope Decision Memorandum to address these comments and set aside a period of time for parties to address scope issues in scope-specific case and rebuttal briefs.
[
4
]
We received no comments from parties on the Preliminary Scope Decision Memorandum. Therefore, we made no changes to the scope of the investigation as it appeared in the
Initiation Notice. See
the scope in Appendix I to this notice.
Verification
As provided in section 782(i) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), in June and July 2026, Commerce verified the sales and cost information submitted by Borregaard AS (Borregaard), for use in our final determination. We used standard verification procedures, including an examination of relevant sales and accounting records, and original source documents provided by Borregaard.
[
5
]
Analysis of Comments Received
All issues raised in the case and rebuttal briefs submitted by interested parties in this investigation are addressed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum. For a list of the issues addressed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum, see Appendix II.
Changes Since the Preliminary Determination
We made certain changes to the margin calculations for Borregaard since the
Preliminary Determination.
For a discussion of these changes,
see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.
All-Others Rate
Section 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act and Commerce's regulations at
19 CFR 351.109(f)(1)
provide that Commerce shall determine an estimated weighted-average dumping margin,
i.e.,
all-others rate, for all exporters and producers not individually examined. This rate shall be an amount equal to the weighted average of the estimated weighted-average dumping margins established for exporters and producers individually investigated, excluding any zero and
de minimis
margins, and any margins determined entirely under section 776 of the Act.
In this investigation, Commerce calculated an individual estimated weighted-average dumping margin for Borregaard. Because Borregaard's estimated weighted-average dumping margin is the only individually calculated rate in this investigation and it is not zero,
de minimis,
or based entirely on facts otherwise available, the rate calculated for Borregaard is also the estimated weighted-average dumping margin assigned to all other producers and exporters not individually examined, pursuant to section 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act.

, in accordance with

Continuation of Suspension of Liquidation and Cash Deposit Requirements
In accordance with section 735(c)(1)(B) of the Act, Commerce will instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to continue to suspend liquidation of all entries of subject merchandise entries, as described in Appendix I of this notice, which were entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after May 27, 2026, the date of publication of the
Preliminary Determination
in the

19 CFR 351.210(d)

ITC Notification
In accordance with section 735(d) of the Act, we will notify the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) of our final affirmative determination of sales at LTFV. Because the final determination in this proceeding is affirmative, in accordance with section 735(b)(2) of the Act, the ITC will determine, within 45 days, whether the domestic industry in the United States is materially injured, or threatened with material injury, by reason of imports of high purity dissolving pulp from Norway. If the ITC determines that material injury or threat of material injury does not exist, the proceeding will be terminated, all cash deposits will be refunded, and suspension of liquidation will be lifted. If the ITC determines that such injury does exist, Commerce will issue an antidumping duty order directing CBP to assess, upon further instruction by Commerce, antidumping duties on all imports of the subject merchandise that are entered, or

Notification to Interested Parties

19 CFR 351.210(c)

Appendix I
Scope of the Investigation
The merchandise subject to this investigation is high purity dissolving pulp, which is a dissolving pulp with an alpha cellulose percentage of 90 percent by weight or higher on an oven dry basis, as calculated by: alpha cellulose percentage = (100−S10) + 0.5 * (S10−S18) where S10 and S18 values are determined by International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 692:1982, and having a brightness level of 90 percent or higher, as measured by ISO 2470-1:2016. High purity dissolving pulp may be derived from any virgin or recycled cellulose fiber source (including, but not limited to, those sourced from hardwoods, softwoods, woody crops, agricultural crops/byproducts/residue, and agricultural/industrial/other waste). High purity dissolving pulp may be produced from a chemical pulping process including without limitation a kraft (sulfate) pulping and/or sulfite pulping process.
High purity dissolving pulp can be shipped in any form, including, but not limited to, a liquid slurry or in any dried form such as flakes, powder, granules, pellets, shreds, rolls and sheets.
The scope includes merchandise matching the above description that has been finished, packaged, or otherwise processed in a third country, including but not limited to processes such as commingling, blending, diluting, repackaging, or any other process that would not otherwise remove the merchandise from the scope of the investigation if performed in the subject country. The scope also includes high purity dissolving pulp that is commingled or blended with high purity dissolving pulp from sources not subject to this investigation. Only the subject component of such commingled or blended products is covered by the scope of this investigation.
Excluded from the scope is high purity dissolving pulp with an intrinsic viscosity under 455 milliliters per gram (mL/g), as measured by ISO 5351:2010.
Also excluded from the scope is cotton linters pulp that consists of at least 90 percent by weight, on an oven-dried basis, of cotton linters fibers.
High purity dissolving pulp products are classified under subheadings 4702.00.0020 and 4702.00.0040 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS). High purity dissolving pulp products may also enter under subheadings 4706.30.0000 or 4706.92.0100. Reference to the HTSUS classifications is provided for convenience and customs purposes, and the written description of the merchandise under investigation is dispositive.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) determines that high purity dissolving pulp (dissolving pulp) from Brazil is being, or is likely to be, sold in the United States at less than fair value (LTFV). The period of investigation (POI) is July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025.
DATES:
Applicable October 16, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ian Riggs, AD/CVD Operations, Office IX, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-3810.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On May 27, 2026, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the preliminary affirmative determination in the LTFV investigation of dissolving pulp from Brazil and postponed the final determination until 135 days after the date of publication of the
Preliminary Determination.
[
1
]
Accordingly, the deadline for this final determination is now October 9, 2026. We invited interested parties to comment on the
Preliminary Determination.
[
2
]
A summary of the events that occurred since Commerce published the
Preliminary Determination,
as well as a full discussion of the issues raised by parties for this final determination, may be found in the Issues and Decision Memorandum.
[
3
]
The Issues and Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS). ACCESS is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov
.
In addition, a complete version of the Issues and Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/​frnotices
.
Scope of the Investigation
The product covered by this investigation is dissolving pulp from Brazil. For a complete description of the scope of this investigation,
see
Appendix I.
Scope Comments
In the Preliminary Scope Memorandum, we set aside a period of time for parties to raise issues regarding product coverage (
i.e.,
scope) in scope-specific case briefs or other written comments.
[
4
]
We received no scope case briefs from interested parties. Therefore, we made no changes to the scope of the investigation as it appeared in the
Preliminary Determination.
Verification
As provided in section 782(i) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), in June and July 2026 Commerce conducted verifications of the sales and cost information submitted by Bracell Bahia Specialty Celulose S.A. and Bracell SP Celulose Ltda. (collectively, Bracell) for use in the final determination. We used standard verification procedures, including an examination of relevant sales and accounting records, and original source documents provided by Bracell.
(
printed page 65724)
Analysis of Comments Received
All issues raised in the case and rebuttal briefs submitted by interested parties in this investigation are addressed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum. For a list of the issues addressed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum,
see

Changes Since the Preliminary Determination
We made certain changes to the calculation of the estimated weighted-average dumping margin for Bracell since the
Preliminary Determination.
For a discussion of these changes,
see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.
All-Others Rate
Section 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act provides that Commerce shall determine an estimated weighted-average dumping margin,
i.e.,
all-others rate, for all exporters and producers not individually examined. This rate shall be an amount equal to the weighted average of the estimated weighted-average dumping margins established for exporters and producers individually investigated, excluding any zero and
de minimis
margins, and any margins determined entirely under section 776 of the Act.
In this investigation, Commerce calculated an individual estimated weighted-average dumping margin for Bracell. Because Bracell's estimated weighted-average dumping margin is the only individually calculated rate in this investigation and it is not zero,
de minimis,
or based entirely on facts otherwise available, the rate calculated for Bracell is also the estimated weighted-average dumping margin assigned to all other producers and exporters.

In accordance with section 735(c)(1)(B) of the Act, Commerce will instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to continue to suspend liquidation of all entries of subject merchandise, as described in Appendix I of this notice, which were entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after May 27, 2026, the date of publication of the

U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) Notification
In accordance with section 735(d) of the Act, Commerce will notify the ITC of our final affirmative determination of sales at LTFV. Because the final determination in this proceeding is affirmative, in accordance with sections 735(b)(2) of the Act, the ITC will make its final determination as to whether the domestic industry in the United States is materially injured, or threatened with material injury, by reason of imports of dissolving pulp from Brazil no later than 45 days after this final determination. Appendix I
The merchandise subject to this investigation is high purity dissolving pulp, which is a dissolving pulp with an alpha
(
printed page 65725)
cellulose percentage of 90 percent by weight or higher on an oven dry basis, as calculated by: alpha cellulose percentage = (100−S10) + 0.5 * (S10−S18) where S10 and S18 values are determined by International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 692:1982, and having a brightness level of 90 percent or higher, as measured by ISO 2470-1:2016. High purity dissolving pulp may be derived from any virgin or recycled cellulose fiber source (including, but not limited to, those sourced from hardwoods, softwoods, woody crops, agricultural crops/byproducts/residue, and agricultural/industrial/other waste). High purity dissolving pulp may be produced from a chemical pulping process including without limitation a kraft (sulfate) pulping and/or sulfite pulping process.
High purity dissolving pulp can be shipped in any form, including, but not limited to, a liquid slurry or in any dried form such as flakes, powder, granules, pellets, shreds, rolls and sheets.
The scope includes merchandise matching the above description that has been finished, packaged, or otherwise processed in a third country, including but not limited to processes such as commingling, blending, diluting, repackaging, or any other process that would not otherwise remove the merchandise from the scope of the investigation if performed in the subject country. The scope also includes high purity dissolving pulp that is commingled or blended with high purity dissolving pulp from sources not subject to this investigation. Only the subject component of such commingled or blended products is covered by the scope of this investigation.
Excluded from the scope is high purity dissolving pulp with an intrinsic viscosity under 455 milliliters per gram (mL/g), as measured by ISO 5351:2010.
Also excluded from the scope is cotton linters pulp that consists of at least 90 percent by weight, on an oven-dried basis, of cotton linters fibers.
High purity dissolving pulp products are classified under subheadings 4702.00.0020 and 4702.00.0040 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS). High purity dissolving pulp products may also enter under subheadings 4706.30.0000 or 4706.92.0100. Reference to the HTSUS classifications is provided for convenience and customs purposes, and the written description of the merchandise under investigation is dispositive.
